Since considerable data indicate that the scrapie
isoform of the prion protein, by analogy the CJD isoform,
is required for infectivity,96,97 we would expect that all cases
of authentic, noninherited CJD will contain the proteaseresistant isoforms of the human prion protein. In support of this argument that all cases of CJD should
have demonstrable CJD prion proteins is our experience
with the immunostaining of CJD amyloid plaques. In 16
(94%) of 17 CJD cases with amyloid plaques we have found
PrP immunoreactive plaques.46,98,99 Since all cases of CJD
do not have readily identifiable amyloid plaques, immu¬
nostaining of tissue sections fixed in formaldehyde and em¬
bedded in paraffin is only useful when positive. The use of
other fixatives such as McLean's appears to be superior to
formaldehyde in preserving PrP antigenicity.100
IATROGENIC CREUTZFELDT-JAKOB DISEASE
Accidental transmission of CJD to humans appears to have
occurred with corneal transplantation,101 contaminated elec¬
troencephalographic electrode implantation,102 and surgi¬
cal operations using contaminated instruments or appa¬
ratus (Table 5) ,77·103-105 Corneas unknowingly removed from
donors with CJD have been transplanted to apparently healthy
recipients who developed CJD after prolonged incubation
periods. Corneas of animals have significant levels of pri¬
ons,106 making this scenario seem quite probable. The same
improperly decontaminated electroencephalographic elec¬
trodes that caused CJD in two young patients with intrac¬
table epilepsy were found to cause CJD in a chimpanzee
18 months after their experimental implantation.107
Surgical procedures may have resulted in accidental
inoculation of patients with prions during their opera¬
tions,23'04,108 presumably because some instrument or ap¬
paratus in the operating theater became contaminated when
a CJD patient underwent surgery. Although the epidemi¬
ology ofthese studies is highly suggestive, no prooffor such
episodes exists. Table 4.

4 days for 4 to 12 years.25
'19127 Interestingly, most patients

presented with cerebellar syndromes that progressed over

How many lots of the HGH might have been contaminated

developing symptoms. Thus, we estimate that one per 104
dead people have CJD. Since 10 000 human pituitary glands
were typically processed in a single HGH preparation, the

prions is not remote.

KURU
For many decades, kuru devastated the lives of the Fore
Highlanders of Papua-New Guinea.23 The high incidence
of the disease among women left a society of motherless
children raised by their fathers (Table 5). It was unusual
to see an older woman in the Fore region. With the ces¬
sation of traditional warfare, older men are now found.

text:
It was unusual
to see an older woman in the Fore region. With the ces¬
sation of traditional warfare, older men are now found. Many
of these older men have had a succession of wives, each
dying of kuru after leaving several children. Because con¬
tamination during ritualistic cannibalism appears to have
been the mode of spread of kuru among the Fore people,
and since cannibalism had ceased by 1960 in the Fore re¬
gion, the patients now developing kuru presumably were
exposed to the kuru agent more than two decades ago.22,23
In many cases, histories from patients and their families of
the episode in which they cannibalized the remains of a
near relative who had died of kuru have been obtained,
presumably providing the source ofinfection. That the kuru
prions could remain apparently quiescent in these patients
for periods of three decades128 and then manifest themselves
in the form of a fatal neurologic disease is supported by
incubation periods of over 7.5 years in some monkeys in¬
oculated with kuru agent.143
Uniformity of Clinical Signs
The uniform clinical presentation ofkuru is remarkable.144-149
The prodromal symptoms and onset of the disease were
similar in all of the patients investigated in one study.128
Even the time interval between the prodromal symptoms
of headache andjoint pain and the onset ofdifficulty walk¬
ing was always 6 to 12 weeks. In most cases, the disease
progressed to death within 12 months, and all patients were
dead within 2 years of onset. The average duration of ill—
nessforthe 15 patients was 16 months.128 Invariably, signs
of cerebellar dysfunction dominated the clinical picture. All patients remained ambulatory with the aid of a stick for
more than half of the clinical phase of their illness.

source: Genetic and Infectious Prion Diseases (Prusiner, S. B) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
The average duration of ill—
nessforthe 15 patients was 16 months.128 Invariably, signs
of cerebellar dysfunction dominated the clinical picture. All patients remained ambulatory with the aid of a stick for
more than half of the clinical phase of their illness. These
clinical characteristics were similar to those reported for
adult patients at the peak of the kuru epidemic.144"149
There has been debate about dementia in kuru.144"149
Findings of memory loss and disorientation accompanied
by primitive reflexes such as snout, bite, suck, rooting, and
hand grasps leave no doubt that patients become demented
at an advanced stage of the disease.128 The same patients
also exhibited considerable muscle paratonia or gegenhalten. The uniformity of presentation and clinical course in
kuru contrasts with that of CJD, in which a wide spectrum
of clinical manifestations is found.150·151 While most CJD
patients exhibit dementia, myoclonus, and pyramidal tract
dysfunction at an early stage of the clinical illness, 10% to
20% present with an ataxic illness.152,153 However, the de¬
mentia appears at an earlier clinical stage in ataxic CJD than
in kuru. During the ambulatory phase of disease, no pa¬
tients with kuru were found to be as severely demented as
are most patients with CJD. Incubation Periods That Exceed Three Decades
No individual born in the South Fore region after 1959
has developed kuru. Kuru has progressively disappeared,
Downloaded From: http://archneur.jamanetwork.com/ by a Michigan State University User on 06/16/2015
first among children and thereafter among adolescents. The
number of deaths in adult females has decreased steadily,
and adult male deaths have remained almost invariant.

source: Genetic and Infectious Prion Diseases (Prusiner, S. B) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf

Kuru has progressively disappeared,
Downloaded From: http://archneur.jamanetwork.com/ by a Michigan State University User on 06/16/2015
first among children and thereafter among adolescents. The
number of deaths in adult females has decreased steadily,
and adult male deaths have remained almost invariant. No
one born in a village since cannibalism ceased has ever de¬
veloped kuru.22,62 Each year the youngest new patients are
older than those of the previous year.130
Of several hundred kuru orphans born since 1957 to
mothers dying of kuru, none has yet developed the dis¬
ease. Thus, the many children with kuru seen in the 1950s
were not infected prenatally, perinatally, or neonatally by
their mothers. There is no evidence for transmission in utero
or by human milk. The regular disappearance of kuru is
inconsistent with the existence of any natural reservoirs for
kuru besides humans. Indeed, there is no evidence for ani¬
mal or insect reservoirs. While patients currently afflicted with kuru exhibit
greatly prolonged incubation periods, children with kuru
who were observed 20 years ago provide some informa¬
tion on the minimum incubation period. The youngest pa¬
tient with kuru was 4 years old at the onset of the disease
and died at age 5. It is not known at what age young chil¬
dren were infected. Accidental transmission of CJD to hu¬
mans has required only 18 months after intracerebral or
intraoptic inoculation.101·102 An incubation period of 18 months
has also been found in chimpanzees inoculated intracerebrally with the kuru agent.

It is not known at what age young chil¬
dren were infected. Accidental transmission of CJD to hu¬
mans has required only 18 months after intracerebral or
intraoptic inoculation.101·102 An incubation period of 18 months
has also been found in chimpanzees inoculated intracerebrally with the kuru agent. Transmission by Cannibalism
Considerable evidence implicates ritualistic cannibalism as
the mode oftransmission for kuru among the Fore and neigh¬
boring tribes.23 Oral transmission of kuru to monkeys has
been documented.143 Proposed transmission routes through
laceration of the skin and rubbing of the eyes remains to
be established.23 These routes were suggested when early
experiments on oral transmission to apes and monkeys failed. The experimental results from oral transmission of scrapie
to hamsters suggests that insufficient doses of the kuru agent
or prion were used in those protocols.36
Origin of Kuru
It has been suggested that kuru began at the turn of the
century as a spontaneous case of CJD that was propagated
by ritualistic cannibalism.22,23 Whether the Fore peoples
and their immediate neighbors provide an especially per¬
missive genetic background on which kuru prions mul¬
tiply remains to be established. Sequencing of the ORF of
the PrP gene from three kuru patients failed to reveal any
mutations.154 Noteworthy is a case of CJD outside the kuru
region in Papua-New Guinea. Transmission to Animals
Kuru has been regularly transmitted after intracerebral in¬
oculation to apes and monkeys.25,31 Occasional cases have
been transmitted to cats but not to rodents.80 The prolonged
incubation periods in experimental animals are similar to
those observed with CJD and GSS (Table 4). Oral trans¬
mission of kuru to apes and monkeys has been difficult,23
but recent studies have demonstrated transmission to mon¬
keys.

source: Genetic and Infectious Prion Diseases (Prusiner, S. B) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
Oral trans¬
mission of kuru to apes and monkeys has been difficult,23
but recent studies have demonstrated transmission to mon¬
keys. 145 Presumably, the difficulties transmitting human kuru
prions to apes and monkeys orally are due to the ineffi¬
ciency of this route36 and the crossing of a species barrier. Immunologie and Molecular Biological Studies
Using PrP antiserum, protease-resistant immunoreactive pro¬
teins have been demonstrated in the brain extracts of one
(50%) of two patients dying of kuru.91 Presumably, these
two patients are included in a larger series where three (75%)
of four kuru patients were found to have the abnormal isoforms of the prion protein.95
DNA sequencing of the ORF of the PrP gene from pa¬
tients dying of kuru has failed to reveal any mutations.154
This finding is consistent with the postulate that kuru was
transmitted by ritualistic cannibalism. GERSTMANN-STRÄUSSLER-SCHEINKER DISEASE
Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker disease, also known as
Sträussler's disease and Gerstmann-Sträusslersyndrome, was
first described by Gerstmann and coworkers in 1936.155
This syndrome originally referred to a familial condition,
but sporadic cases resembling GSS clinically and patho¬
logically have been reported and are now generally included
under the same rubric.11156 The different clinical presen¬
tations of GSS suggested that it may be a heterogeneous
disorder and it was defined as a "spinocerebellar ataxia with
dementia and plaquelike deposits."157
Molecular genetic investigations of GSS have defined
four syndromes each with a different PRNP gene point mu¬
tation (Table 6). The ataxic form of GSS is caused by a
point mutation at codon 102,48 while a telencephalic form
is caused by a mutation at codon 117.

Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker disease is rare.1U561b2165
This disease comprises less than 2% of nearly 1000 cases
of CJD or CJD-related diseases.11 Assuming that the inci¬
dence of CJD is less than one per million, a rough estimate
of the incidence of GSS is less than two per 100 million. This estimate mayunderrepresent GSS, since GSS frequently

All reported cases of GSS have originated in the north¬

text:
Clinical Features
The diversity ofclinical manifestations in GSS, even within
the same pedigree, is well documented; however, patients
typically complain of difficulty walking and unsteadiness,
sometimes accompanied by leg pains or paresthesias in the
early stages of the disease. On examination, cerebellar ataxia,
dysarthria, ocular dysmetria, hyporeflexia or areflexia in
the lower extremities with extensor plantar responses, and
mild wasting or weakness in the lower extremities may be
found. Hyporeflexia or areflexia in the lower extremities
may be helpful in distinguishing GSS from dominantly in¬
herited olivopontocerebellar degeneration. Sensory distur¬
bances, usually impairment of vibratory and propioceptive sensations, are occasionally detected on examination. Later in the course, mental deterioration may occur; some¬
times it is quite mild or is difficult to assess because of se¬
vere dysarthria. Dysphagia frequently develops and con¬
tributes to inanition in the late stages of disease. Deafness,
blindness, gaze palsies, and extrapyramidal rigidity have
been reported in several cases. Convulsions may occur but
are rare. Myoclonus seldom occurs, and, when it does, it
may be confined to the lower extremities. The majority ofpatients present with symptoms in the
fourth to sixth decades. The average age of onset is 43 years
old and ranges from 24 to 66 years old. Symptoms may
initially be relapsing, and, thus, GSS can be mistaken for
multiple sclerosis. Eventually, inexorable progression ofsymp¬
toms leads to death. The duration of illness ranges from 1
to 11 years with a mean of 5 years. The mean age at death
is 48 years. The age of onset may vary as much as three
decades within a single pedigree.164
Clinically, GSS is thought to be distinguished from
CJD by the prominence ofataxia in the former and the promi¬
nence of dementia with myoclonus in the latter.

source: Genetic and Infectious Prion Diseases (Prusiner, S. B) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf

The mean age at death
is 48 years. The age of onset may vary as much as three
decades within a single pedigree.164
Clinically, GSS is thought to be distinguished from
CJD by the prominence ofataxia in the former and the promi¬
nence of dementia with myoclonus in the latter. Yet, para¬
doxically, the clinical manifestations of both GSS and CJD
may occur in different members of the same family. In one
such family, the characteristic amyloid plaques ofGSS were
found in all afflicted members, including one member who
died with a rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus
clinically consistent with CJD ,1 ',75 This patient's father and
sister had both been afflicted with slowly progressive ataxia
and little or no accompanying dementia as is characteristic
for GSS. Such a pedigree raises the question of whether
CJD and GSS are distinct entities and, perhaps, demon¬
strates how a single alíele can be variably expressed against
different genetic backgrounds. Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker disease and kuru are
different in duration ofclinical illness (up to 5 years in GSS
vs 1 to 2 years in kuru), morphologic appearance of amy¬
loid plaques (multicentric in GSS vs unincentric in kuru),
and mode of transmission (vertical in GSS vs horizontal in
kuru). However, the symptomatology and distribution of
neuropathologic lesions in GSS and kuru are strikingly simi¬
lar, thus also calling into question whether they are sepa¬
rate diseases. Genetics and Diagnostic Evaluation
Most cases of GSS are familial," exhibiting an autosomal
dominant pattern with nearly complete penetrance. The
premortem diagnosis of GSS is secure if a nonconservative
mutation of the PrP gene is found.27 Prior to the discovery
of PrP gene mutations causing GSS, the diagnosis of GSS
was rarely made prior to autopsy. Biopsy of the cerebellum
was occasionally diagnostic when PrP amyloid plaques were
found.

source: Genetic and Infectious Prion Diseases (Prusiner, S. B) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
The
premortem diagnosis of GSS is secure if a nonconservative
mutation of the PrP gene is found.27 Prior to the discovery
of PrP gene mutations causing GSS, the diagnosis of GSS
was rarely made prior to autopsy. Biopsy of the cerebellum
was occasionally diagnostic when PrP amyloid plaques were
found. Serologie and cerebrospinal fluid examinations show
normal findings. Computed axial tomography ofthe brain
sometimes reveals cerebellar and brain-stem atrophy. The
electroencephalogram is normal or shows nonspecific, dif¬
fuse changes. Periodic complexes have not been reported
in GSS, except in those cases whose clinical manifestations
resembled CJD. Electromyography may reveal denervation
potentials in lumbosacral myotomes. Sensory and motor
nerve conduction velocities are normal. Transmission to Animals
In 1978, Tateishi and coworkers166,167 produced experimen¬
tal spongiform encephalopathy in mice and rats using brain
tissue from a patient with a chronic spongiform encepha¬
lopathy and kuru plaques.166,167 Although this case was not
thought to be familial at the time, its clinicopathologic fea¬
tures resembled GSS, and, subsequently, Masters and coworkers" suggested that this case be classified as GSS.

In
1981, transmission of GSS to monkeys using brain tissue
from a patient with familial disease was reported." Sub¬
sequently, brain tissue from another afflicted member of
the same family was used to transmit disease to marmoDownloaded From: http://archneur.jamanetwork.com/ by a Michigan State University User on 06/16/2015
sets.168 No diagnostic conclusions can as yet be made from
such transmission studies because transmissibility of GSS
appears to be variable, even within a single pedigree.11,168
Immunologie Studies
Using PrP antiserum, protease-resistant immunoreactive pro¬
teins have been demonstrated in the brain extracts of two
(50%) of four patients with GSS.91 Presumably, these two
patients are included in a second report where three (75%)
of four GSS patients were stated to have the abnormal isoforms ofthe prionprotein.95 Partiallypurified protease-resistant
prion proteins from the brain of one patient dying of GSS
were to found be PrP immunoreactive on Western immunoblots.92 Subsequent studies with larger numbers of GSS
patients have documented the PrP immunoreactivity ofamy¬
loid plaques and the presence of PrP*.16917° A dot blot pro¬
cedure for detection ofPrP* in brain homogenates provides
a rapid and reliable method for the diagnosis of GSS pro¬
vided multiple regions of the brain are sampled.93 Isola¬
tion of amyloid plaques from the brains of GSS patients
and subsequent purification of a major 11-kd protein has
shown by protein sequencing that this protein is a proteolytic
fragment of PrP extending from residue 58 to 150.171
NEUROPATHOLOGY OF
THE HUMAN PRION DISEASES
The triad ofmicroscopic features that characterize the prion
diseases consists of (1) spongiform degeneration of neu¬
rons, (2) severe astrocytic gliosis that often appears to be
out of proportion to the degree of nerve cell loss, and (3)
amyloid plaque formation (Figure |) n^432152·172-175
Spongiform degeneration consists ofintracellular vacu¬
oles that focally dilate neuronal processes, giving the gray
matter a microvacuolated appearance by light microscopy.

source: Genetic and Infectious Prion Diseases (Prusiner, S. B) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
Ultrastructurally, the vacuoles display splitting of the unit
cell membrane with the formation ofblisterlike membrane
expansions and multiple septae.175 In addition, the abnor¬
mal single-component membranes are focally thickened and
necrotic. These neuronal membrane alterations as primary
targets of the disease strongly correlate with the prion pro¬
tein being an integral membrane sialoglycoprotein,8,10·41,42'139·176
which, during the course ofthe disease, accumulates in neu¬
ronal cell membranes. Neuropathology of CJD
Frequently, the brains of patients with CJD show no rec¬
ognizable abnormalities on gross examination. In patients
surviving several years, variable degrees of cerebral atro¬
phy are likely to result in brain weights as low as 850 g. The pathologic hallmarks ofCJD at the light-microscopic
level are spongiform degeneration and astrogliosis. The lack
of an inflammatory response in CJD and other prion dis¬
eases is an important pathologic feature of these degenerarive disorders. Generally, the spongiform changes occur in
the cerebral cortex, putamen, caudate nucleus, thalamus,
and molecular layer of the cerebellum.177"179 Spongiform
degeneration is characterized by many 1- to 5-µ vacu¬
oles in the neuropil between nerve cell bodies.77 By elec¬
tron microscopy, the vacuoles appear to be swollen neu¬
ronal processes and seem to be surrounded by a mem¬
brane.178,180 Frequently, many membrane fragments can be
seen within them. In some brains with CJD, we have seen
no recognizable spongilorm degeneration. Generally, the
white matter is devoid of lesions, but several cases of CJD
inJapan have exhibited well-documented vacuolarchanges.181
In natural scrapie ofsheep, vacuolization is very limited,182
while experimental scrapie of rodents is accompanied by
widespread vacuolar changes. In TME, there is generally
widespread vacuolation, but infected Aleutian mink fail to
show vacuolar change.183 Thus, vacuolation, while a com¬
mon feature ofprion diseases, does not seem to be an obliga¬
tory change.

source: Genetic and Infectious Prion Diseases (Prusiner, S. B) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf

In TME, there is generally
widespread vacuolation, but infected Aleutian mink fail to
show vacuolar change.183 Thus, vacuolation, while a com¬
mon feature ofprion diseases, does not seem to be an obliga¬

specific, of prion diseases. Widespread proliferation of fi¬
brous astrocytes is found throughout the gray matter ofbrains
infected with CJD prions. Astrocytic processes filled with

CJD. Purified CJD prions from humans and animals ex¬

of amyloid.90,138 In first passage from some human Japa¬
nese CJD cases, amyloid plaques have been found in mouse
brains.184 These plaques stain with antisera raised against
scrapie hamster PrP 27-30 protein.46,98,99,185
The majority of cases of kuru show plaques that are
presumably comprised of amyloid within their cores.69,179
The kuru plaques differ from senile plaques in that senile
plaques have a collection of amorphous material, presum¬
ably degenerating dendrites, around their amyloid core. The
kuru plaques do not possess such a large halo.

The
kuru plaques do not possess such a large halo. Both kuru
and senile plaques have been reported in CJD, but they are
not a constant feature of the disease.186,187 Kuru plaques do
seem to be a constant feature of GSS.11,188
Neuropathology of GSS
The neuropathologic diagnosis of GSS is based on the pres¬
ence of characteristic amyloid plaque deposition, degen¬
eration of white matter tracts, and neuronal loss through¬
out the brain, variably accompanied by spongiform changes
and gliosis. The distribution and extent ofthese neuropatho¬
logic changes differs widely between patients, even within
one pedigree. The amyloid plaques of GSS are distinct from those
seen in kuru, AD, or scrapie. The GSS plaques consist of
a central dense core ofamyloid surrounded by smaller glob¬
ules of amyloid. Ultrastructurally, they consist of a radi¬
ating fibrillar network of amyloid fibrils with scant or no
neuritic degeneration. The plaques can be distributed through¬
out the brain but are most frequently found in the cerebel¬
lum. They are often located adjacent to blood vessels. Congophilic angiopathy has been noted in some cases of GSS. In addition to the multicentric plaques of GSS, unicentric
kuru plaques may also be seen."
In numerous cases ofGSS, there are PrP-immunoreactive
proteins within the amyloid plaques.98,99,189 Thus, like CJD
and kuru, the amyloid plaques of GSS specifically stain with
antisera raised against PrP 27-30 that was isolated from scrapieinfected hamster brains. The PrP immunostaining of formalinfixed brain tissue embedded in paraffin blocks as well as
dot blot immunostaining of PrP* in brain homogenates can
be used to establish the diagnosis of GSS.93,98
The pattern of white matter degeneration resembles
that of other systems degeneration, such as hereditary spino¬
cerebellar degeneration (Friedreich's), cerebellar degenera¬
tion (Marie), and dentatorubral degeneration (Ramsay-Hunt).

source: Genetic and Infectious Prion Diseases (Prusiner, S. B) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
The principal tracts involved include the dorsal and ven¬
tral spinocerebellar tracts; the posterior columns; the su¬
perior, middle, and inferior cerebellar peduncles; and the
corticospinal tracts. Neuronal loss occurs in scattered areas throughout the
brain and spinal cord. The nuclei and regions that may be
affected include Clarke's column; anterior horn cells; ves¬
tibular and cochlear nuclei; dentate nuclei; Purkinje and
granule cells in the cerebellum, pontine nuclei, inferior ol¬
ive, thalamus, substantia nigra, striatum, globus pallidus,
and subthalamic nucleus; and all layers of the cerebral cor¬
tex and hippocampus. The presence of spongiform changes can vary even
within a given pedigree." Transmission of GSS to experi¬
mental animals wasachievedonlyin caseswith severespongi¬
form changes'
' until Tateishi and coworkers 19° demonstrated
transmission to rodents from a case of GSS with minimal
spongiform changes. Prior to the availability ofimmunocytochemical analy¬
ses for PrP, some cases of GSS were incorrectly diagnosed
as familial AD, since histochemistry showed NFTs and amy¬
loid plaques of the Alzheimer type.165,191 While NFTs con¬
fined to the hippocampus may be incidental, the distribu¬
tion ofNFTs throughout the cerebral cortexalongwith plaques
suggests AD or the simultaneous occurrence ofAD and GSS.165
Subsequent immunostaining studies have showed that the
amyloid plaques in some of these cases are composed of
prion proteins and do not bind antibodies raised to the
ß-amyloid peptide.192"195 Molecular genetic investigations
elucidated the point mutations of the PrP gene in each of
these prion disorders. Neuropathology of Kuru
The neuropathologic changes in kuru are much like those
described for CJD and GSS. Spongiform changes, astrogliosis, and amyloid or "kuru" plaques are the pathologic hall¬
marks of kuru.

Neuropathology of Kuru
The neuropathologic changes in kuru are much like those
described for CJD and GSS. Spongiform changes, astrogliosis, and amyloid or "kuru" plaques are the pathologic hall¬
marks of kuru. Most, but not all, cases ofkuru exhibit amy¬
loid plaques.69 These plaques have been found to contain
prion proteins by immunostaining.99
MOLECULAR GENETICS OF
INHERITED HUMAN PRION DISEASES
Human PrP Gene Mutations
In humans, genetics were first thought to have a role in
CJD with the recognition that approximately 10% of cases
are familial.23,24 Like sheep scrapie, the relative contribu¬
tions of genetic and infectious causes in the human prion
diseases remained puzzling. The discovery of the PrP gene
raised the possibility that mutation might feature in the he¬
reditary human prion diseases. A point mutation at codon
102 (P—>L) was shown to be linked genetically to devel¬
opment ofGSS with a Lod score exceeding 3 (Figure 2).48
This mutation may be due to the deamination of a methy¬
lated CpG in a germline PrP gene, resulting in the substi¬
tution of a for C. The codon 102 mutation has been found
in ten different families in nine different countries includ¬
ing the original GSS family (Table )."«*."*

Human PrP Gene Polymorphisms
At PrP codon 129, an amino acid (Met/Val) polymorphism
(Figure 2) has been identified.234 Patients with CJD fol¬
lowing treatment with human pituitary growth hor¬
mone26,117 or gonadotropin have a significant preponder¬
ance of the Val alíele235 compared with the general population
(Table 8). Sporadic CJD patients were found to be homozygous for the Met or Val alíele at codon 129 but were
rarely heterozygous.236 This finding was interpreted236,237
as consistent with the hypothesis that PrPc/PrPSt heterodimers feature in the replication of prions.2,238
TRANSMISSION OF NEUROLOGIC DISEASE
TO RODENTS FROM TG MICE EXPRESSING
GSS MUTANT MOPRP(PIOIL)
The codon 102 point mutation found in GGS patients was
introduced into the MoPrP gene and Tg(MoPrP-P101L)H
mice were created expressing high (H) levels of the mutant
transgene product. The Tg(MoPrP-P101L)H mice sponta¬
neously developed CNS degeneration, characterized by clini¬
cal signs indistinguishable from experimental murine scrapie
andneuropathologic findings consistingofwidespread spongi¬
form morphology and astrocytic gliosis89 and PrP amyloid
plaques. Brain extracts prepared from Tg(MoPrP-P 101L)H
mice transmitted CNS degeneration to inoculated recipi¬
ents. Although inoculated CD-I Swiss mice failed to de¬
velop illness, some SHas and many Tg(MoPrP-P101L)L mice
expressing low (L) levels of the mutant trangene product
did become ill. By inference, these results contend that PrP
mutations cause GSS and familial CJD. It is unclear whether
the low levels of protease-resistant PrP in the brains of Tg
mice with the GSS mutation is PrPSc or residual PrPc. Undetectable or low levels of PrPSc in the brains of these Tg
mice are consistent with the results of transmission experi¬
ments that suggest low titers of infectious prions.

text:
Undetectable or low levels of PrPSc in the brains of these Tg
mice are consistent with the results of transmission experi¬
ments that suggest low titers of infectious prions. These
findings argue that prions are devoid of foreign nucleic acid,
in accord with many studies that use other experimental
approaches.1239-249
One view of the PrP gene mutations has been that they
render individuals susceptible to a common "virus."250"252
In this scenario, the putative scrapie virus is thought to
persist within a worldwide reservoir of humans, animals,
or insects without causing detectable illness. Yet one of
106 individuals develop sporadic CJD and die of a lethal
"infection" while approximately 100% of people with PrP
point mutations or inserts eventually appear to develop
neurologic dysfunction. That germline mutations found
in the PrP genes ofpatients and at-risk individuals are the
cause of familial prion diseases is supported by experi¬
ments with Tg(MoPrP) mice described above.27·253,254 The
Tg mouse studies also argue that sporadic CJD might arise
from the spontaneous conversion of PrPc to PrPCJD due to
either a somatic mutation of the PrP gene or a rare event
involving modification of wild-type PrPc.2

SPECIES BARRIERS IN THE TRANSMISSION
OF PRION DISEASES
Passage of prions between species is a stochastic process
characterized by prolonged incubation times.251"257 Prions
synthesized de novo reflect the sequence of the host PrP
gene and not that of the PrPSc molecules in the inoculum.92
On subsequent passage in a homologous host, the incu¬
bation time shortens to that recorded for all subsequent
passages and it becomes a nonstochastic process. The spe¬
cies barrier concept is of practical importance in assessing
the risk for humans of developing CJD after consumption
of scrapie-infected lamb or BSE beef.

text:
The spe¬
cies barrier concept is of practical importance in assessing
the risk for humans of developing CJD after consumption
of scrapie-infected lamb or BSE beef. To test the hypothesis that differences in PrP gene se¬
quences might be responsible for the species barrier, Tg mice
expressing SHaPrP were constructed.238,2'8 The PrP genes of
SHas and mice encode proteins differing at 16 positions. In¬
cubation times in four lines of Tg(SHaPrP) mice inoculated
with Mo prions were prolonged compared with those ob¬
served for non-Tg, control mice (Figure 3 and Figure 4,
A). Inoculation of Tg(SHaPrP) mice with SHa prions dem¬
onstrated abrogation of the species barrier resulting in ab¬
breviated incubation times due to a nonstochastic process
(Figure 4, B).258,218 The length of the incubation time after
inoculation with SHa prions was inversely proportional to
the level of SHaPrPc in the brains of Tg(SHaPrP) mice (Fig¬
ure 4, and C).238 The SHaPrPbL levels in the brains of clini¬
cally ill mice were similar in all four Tg(SHaPrP) lines in¬
oculated with SHa prions (Figure 4, D). Bioassays of brain
extracts from clinically ill Tg(SHaPrP) mice inoculated with
Mo prions revealed that only Mo prions but no SHa prions
were produced (Figure 4, E). Conversely, inoculation of Tg
(SHaPrP) mice with SHa prions led to only the synthesis of
SHa prions (Figure 4, F). Thus, the de novo synthesis of pri¬
ons is species specific and reflects the genetic origin of the
inoculated prions. Similarly, the neuropathology ofTg(SHaPrP)
mice is determined by the genetic origin ofprion inoculum. Mo prions injected into Tg(SHaPrP) mice produced a neu¬
ropathologic finding characteristic of mice with scrapie. A
moderate degree of vacuolation in both the gray and white
matter was found while amyloid plaques were rarely detected
(Figure 4, G) (Table 9).

text:
To date, the function
of PrPc remains unknown. PRION DIVERSITY
There is good evidence for multiple "strains" or distinct iso¬
lates of prions as defined by specific incubation times, dis¬
tribution of vacuolar lesions, and patterns of PrPSc
accumulation.260263 The mechanism bywhich isolate-specific
information is carried by prions remains enigmatic; indeed,
explaining the molecular basis of prion diversity seems to
be a formidable challenge. For many years, some investi¬
gators argued that scrapie is caused by a viruslike particle
that contains a scrapie-specific nucleic acid that encodes
the information expressed by each isolate.264 To date, no
such polynucleotide has been identified by a wide variety
of techniques including measurements of the nucleic acids
in purified preparations. An alternative hypothesis has been
suggested where PrPSc alone is capable of transmitting dis¬
ease but the characteristics of PrPSc might be modified by
a cellular RNA.40 This accessory cellular RNA is postulated
to induce its own synthesis on transmission from one host
to another. Two additional hypotheses not involving a nucleic acid
have been offered to explain distinct prion isolates: a nonnucleic acid second component might create prion diversity, or posttranslational modification of PrPSc: might be re¬
sponsible for the different properties of distinct prion iso¬
lates.2 Whether the PrPSc modification is chemical or
conformation alone remains to be established, but no can¬
didate chemical modifications have been identified. Struc¬
tural studies of the GPI anchors of two SHa isolates have
failed to reveal any differences; interestingly, about 40% of
the anchor glycans have sialic acid residues (Figure 5).265
A portion of the PrPc GPI anchors also have sialic acid resi¬
dues; PrP is the first protein found to have sialic acid resi¬
dues attached to GPI anchors.

PRION REPLICATION
The mechanism by which prions multiply is unknown. Al¬
though the search for a scrapie-specific nucleic acid contin¬
ues to be unrewarding, some investigators steadfastly cling
to the notion that this putative polynucleotide drives prion
replication. If prions are found to contain a scrapie-specific
nucleic acid, then such a molecule would be expected to di¬
rect scrapie agent replication using a strategy similar to that
employed by viruses (Figure 6, A). In the absence of any
chemical
or physical
evidence
for
a scrapie-specific
polynucleotide,1,239249,270"277 it seems reasonable to consider
some alternative mechanisms that might feature in prion bio¬
synthesis. The multiplication of prion infectivity is an ex¬
ponential process in which the posttranslational conversion
of PrPc or a precursor to PrPSc appears to be obligatory.17 As
illustrated in Figure 6, B, PrPSc molecules combine with two

and contrary to predictions, three of the four spontaneously
formed amyloids as shownby electron microscopy and Congo

tides were found to exhibit a secondary structure comprised
largely of ß-sheets. The first of the predicted helices is the
14-residue peptide corresponding to codons 109 through
122; this peptide and the overlapping 15-residue sequence
113 through 127 both form amyloid. The most highly amy¬
loidogenic peptide is the sequence AGAAAAGA, correspond¬
ing to PrP codons 113 through 120. This peptide is in a re¬
gion of PrP that is conserved across all known species. Two
otherpredicted -helicescorresponding to codons 178 through
191 and 202 through 218 form amyloids and exhibit con¬
siderable ß-sheet structure when synthesized as peptides. These findings suggest the possibility that the conversion
of PrPc to PrPSc involves the transition of one or more pu¬

These structural investigations of synthetic PrP pep¬
tides and the correlations between PrP 27-30 secondary
structure and scrapie infectivity offer a structural model
for the conversion of PrPc to PrPSc as well as the replication
ofinfectiousprion particlesinvolving a transition from -helices
to ß-sheets in PrP. Whether any of the synthetic PrP pep¬
tides described here can induce brain degeneration, PrPSc
formation, or prion infectivity is currently being investi¬
gated. Ifadditional data can be obtained to support the hy¬
pothesis set forth here, then it may be useful to examine
other degenerative diseases with respect to proteins under¬
going similar structural changes. The diversity of scrapie prions264,283"283 poses an in¬
teresting conundrum. The finding that the pattern of PrPSc
accumulation in the CNS is characteristic for a particular
strain offers a mechanism for the propagation of distinct
prion isolates.263 In this model, a different set of cells would
propagate each isolate. Whether or not the isolates are tar¬
geted to specific sets of cells by the Asn-linked oligosaccharides of PrP* remains to be established. It is notewor¬
thy that PrPSc synthesis can occur in the absence of Asnlinked glycosylation in scrapie-infected cultured cells286;
further studies are needed to determine the molecular ba¬
sis of the cellular trophism exhibited by prions.

thy that PrPSc synthesis can occur in the absence of Asnlinked glycosylation in scrapie-infected cultured cells286;
further studies are needed to determine the molecular ba¬
sis of the cellular trophism exhibited by prions. Alterna¬
tively, explaining the problem of multiple distinct prion
isolates might be accommodated by multiple PrP* conform¬
er that act as templates for the folding of de novo synthe¬
sized PrP* molecules during prion "replication" (Figure 6,
D). Although both of these proposals are rather unortho¬
dox, they are consistent with observations generated from
Tg(SHaPrP)Mo studies contending that PrP* in the inocu¬
lum binds to homologous PrPc or a precursor to form a
heterodimeric intermediate in the replication process.238
Whether foldases, chaperonins, or other types of molecules
feature in the conversion of the PrPVPrP* heterodimer to
two molecules of PrP* is unknown. The molecular weight
of a PrP* homodimer is consistent with the ionizing ra¬
diation target size of 55 000±9000 d as determined for in¬
fectious pnon particles independent oftheir polymeric form.287
In humans carrying point mutations or inserts in their
PrP genes, mutant PrPc molecules might spontaneously con¬
vert into PrP* (Figure 6, E). While the initial stochastic event
maybe inefficient, once it happens the process becomes autocatalytic. The proposed mechanism is consistent with in¬
dividuals harboring germline mutations who do not develop
CNS dysfunction for decades and with studies on Tg(MoPrPP101L) mice that spontaneously develop CNS degeneration.89
Whether all GSS and familial CJD cases contain infectious
prions or some represent inborn errors of PrP metabolism
in which neither PrP* nor prion infectivity accumulates is
unknown. If the latter is found, then, presumably, mutant
PrPc molecules alone can produce CNS degeneration.

PrPc molecules alone can produce CNS degeneration. Some investigators have suggested that scrapie agent
multiplication proceeds through a crystallization process in¬
volving PrP amyloid formation.288 29° Against this hypoth¬
esis is the absence or rarity ofamyloid plaques in many prion
diseases as well as the inability to identify any amyloidlike
polymers in cultured cells chronicallysynthesizingprions.2,829
'
Purified infectious preparations isolated from scrapie-infected
hamster brains exist as amorphous aggregates; only if PrP*
is exposed to detergents and limited proteolysis does it then
polymerize into prion rods exhibiting the ultrastructural and
tinctorial features ofamyloid.291 Furthermore, dispersion of
prion rods into detergent-lipid-protein complexes results in
a 10- to 100-fold increase in scrapie titer, and no rods could
be identified in these fractions by electron microscopy.292
SOME CONCLUDING REMARKS ON THE
STRUCTURE AND REPLICATION OF PRIONS
Although many experimental studies reviewed above ar¬
gue persuasively that prions are devoid of nucleic acid, the
Downloaded From: http://archneur.jamanetwork.com/ by a Michigan State University User on 06/16/2015
complete structure of the prion particle remains to be es¬
tablished. Whether the enigma ofprion diversity will even¬
tually be shown to depend on an as yet undetected scrapiespecific nucleic acid orit arises through an unorthodox mecha¬
nism such as Asn-linked glycosylation ofPrP* or variations
in PrP* conformation is uncertain. Consider the remote possibility that prions do con¬
tain an as yet undetected polynucleotide; then, presum¬
ably, prion replication would involve a viruslike strategy. The putative scrapie-specific nucleic acid would act as a
template for its own synthesis using cellular polymerases. By an as yet undefined mechanism, the putative scrapiespecific nucleic acid would stimulate the conversion ofPrPc
to PrP*.

text:
The putative scrapie-specific nucleic acid would act as a
template for its own synthesis using cellular polymerases. By an as yet undefined mechanism, the putative scrapiespecific nucleic acid would stimulate the conversion ofPrPc
to PrP*. While this putative scrapie-specific nucleic acid
would provide a plausible explanation for prion diversity,
it would require that this nucleotide sequence be able to
discriminate between SHaPrP and MoPrP in Tg(SHaPrP)
mice. In addition, the putative scrapie-specific nucleic acid
would have to be ubiquitous to explain how sporadic CJD
occurs with an incidence of 1 per 106 all over the planet,293,294
while virtually all people carrying PrP gene mutations de¬
velop prion disease. A more likely scenario is that prions do not contain a
scrapie-specific nucleic acid; rather, they are composed en¬
tirely of PrP* molecules. If this is the case, then the species
barrier for prion transmission, the results with Tg(SHaPrP)
mice, and infectious prions in the brains of patients with in¬
herited prion diseases can be more readily explained. If pri¬
ons are composed entirely of PrP*, then replication must
involve the interaction of nascent PrPc or a precursor with
PjP* 2,238 Although there is no physical data at this time dem¬
onstrating the existence of PrPc/PrP* heterodimers, it is dif¬
ficult to explain the results obtained with Tg(SHaPrP) mice
in studies ofprion replication. Moreover, other studies have
shown that patients homologous for the Met/Val polymor¬
phism at codon 129 are predisposed to sporadic CJD while
those with heterozygous alíeles at codon 129 are relatively
protected.236 These findings have been interpreted as being
consistent with the hypothesis that prion replication is most
efficient when the primary structures of PrPc and PrP* are
the same.

text:
As noted above, although the PrP* model is con¬
sistent with all of the experimental data, it continues to be
problematic with respect to explaining the molecular basis
of multiple distinct scrapie prion isolates or "strains."
The formal possibility remains that prions contain a
second component that is not a nucleic acid. A small polypeptide, a polysaccharide, a lipid-glycan, or a phospholipid/
sterol complex are all possibilities, but there is no evidence
for any of these molecules as prion components at this time. CONCLUSIONS AND PROSPECTIVE
The study of prions has taken several unexpected direc¬
tions over the past few years. The discovery that prion dis¬
eases in humans are uniquely both genetic and infectious
has greatly strengthened and extended the prion concept. To date, 12 different mutations in the human PrP gene all
resulting in nonconservative substitutions have been found
to be linked genetically to or segregate with the inherited
prion diseases. Yet, the transmissible prion particle is com¬
posed largely, if not entirely, of an abnormal isoform of the
prion protein designated PrP*.2 These findings argue that
prion diseases should be considered pseudoinfections, since
the particles transmitting disease appear to be devoid of a
foreign nucleic acid and, thus, differ from all known mi¬
croorganisms as well as viruses and viroids. Because much
information especially about scrapie of rodents has been
derived using experimental protocols adapted from virol¬
ogy, we continue to use terms such as infection, incuba¬
tion period, transmissibility, and end-point titration in stud¬
ies of prion diseases. Although relatively little is known about the replica¬
tion ofprions, Tg mice expressing foreign or mutant PrP genes
now permit virtually all facets of prion diseases to be stud¬
ied and have created a framework for future investigations.

text:
Although relatively little is known about the replica¬
tion ofprions, Tg mice expressing foreign or mutant PrP genes
now permit virtually all facets of prion diseases to be stud¬
ied and have created a framework for future investigations. Furthermore, the structure and organization ofthe PrP gene
suggested that PrP* is derived from PrPc or a precursor by
a posttranslational process. Studies with scrapie-infected cul¬
tured cells have provided much evidence that the conver¬
sion of PrPc to PrP* is a posttranslational process that prob¬
ably occurs in the endocytic pathway. The molecular basis
of the PrP* synthetic process remains to be elucidated, but
extensive protein chemical studies suggest that this process
is likely to involve a conformational change. It seems likely that the principles learned from the study
ofprion diseases will be applicable to elucidating the causes
of more common neurodegenerative diseases. Such disor¬
ders include AD, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Par¬
kinson disease. Since people at risk for inherited prion dis¬
eases can now be identified decades before neurologic dys¬
function is evident, the development of an effective therapy
is imperative. If PrPc can be diminished in humans with¬
out deleterious effects as is the case for Prn-p0/0 mice,21 then
reducing the level of PrP mRNA with antisense oligonucleotides might prove an effective therapeutic maneuver in
delaying the onset of CNS symptoms and signs. The study of prion biology and diseases seems to be
a new and emerging area ofbiomedicai investigation. While
prion biology has its roots in virology, neurology, and neuropathology, its relationships to the disciplines of molecu¬
lar and cell biology as well as protein chemistry have be¬
come evident only recently. Certainly, the possibility that
learning how prions multiply and cause disease will open
up new vistas in biochemistry and genetics seems likely.

views & reviews
NEUROLOGY 199040:1820-1827
Inherited human prion diseases
Karen Hsiao, MD, and Stanley B. Prusiner, MD
Three human neurodegenerative diseases-kuru,
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), and Gerstmann-
Straussler-Scheinker syndrome (GSS)-show clinical
and pathologic characteristics similar to those of
scrapie, a transmissible neurodegenerative disease of
sheep and goats. The term “prion” was introduced to
distinguish the transmissible agent of scrapie from vi-
ruses and viroids.’ Prions are proteinaceous infectious
particles that contain little or no nucleic acid and in
which an aberrant host protein is a major and necessary
component. Detailed biologic and chemical discussions
of prions can be found else~here.~J
Multiple lines of evidence have led to the conclusion
that prions in animals and humans are closely related
(1) transmission of CJD and scrapie to rodents and
primates produce strikingly similar clinical and neuro-
pathologic characteristic^^^^; (2) experimental CJD in
goats is indistinguishable from natural scrapie6; (3)
both CJD and scrapie agents exhibit extreme resistance
to ionizing radiation and are similar in size7-l’J; (4) both
scrapie and CJD agents show similar patterns of inac-
tivation by chaotropic ions, alkali, and heatlJ1; (5) a
protease-resistant isoform of the prion protein (PrP)
accumulates in the brains of patients with kuru, GSS,
and CJDn-15; (6) Western blots of brain tissue from
patients with kuru, GSS, and CJD are positive when
tested against antiserum to PrPlZ-l5; (7) amyloid
plaques in scrapie, CJD, and GSS are antigenically
related as shown by in situ immunohistochemistry
using PrP antiserum16; and (8) there is nearly 90%
conservation of amino acid sequence among hamster,
mouse, and human PrP molecule^.^^-^^ These observa-
tions form the basis for concluding that prions cause
kuru, CJD, and GSS in humans. Modes of transmission.

text:
Modes of transmission. Although experimental
scrapie occurs through horizontal transmission, the
mechanism by which natural scrapie is transmitted is
still under debate.z0.21 Human prion diseases rarely oc-
cur through horizontal transmission, with the excep-
tion of kuru, which appears to have been transmitted
among the Fore-speaking tribes of New Guinea by ritu-
alistic cannibalism (table l).22.23
The only reported cases
of CJD that have been horizontally transmitted have
occurred iatrogenically, resulting from either con-
taminated neurosurgical instruments, corneal trans-
plants, or human growth hormone preparations from
human pituitary extracts.24 The large majority (-90%)
of CJD cases arise sporadically; for these cases no infec-
tious source can be identified, and the disease does not
appear in previous or subsequent generations related to
the ~ a t i e n t . ~ ~ ~ ~ ~
Familial forms of human prion disease constitute 5
to 15% of CJD and most GSS c a ~ e s ? ~ . ~ ~
The exact
incidence of familial prion diseases is unknown but is
estimated to be between 1 and 10 per hundred million. These familial forms are characterized by an autosomal
dominant pattern of inheritance. Yet, experimental
transmission to nonhuman primates and rodents has
demonstrated that familial cases can also be infec-
t i o ~ s .

dominant pattern of inheritance. Yet, experimental
transmission to nonhuman primates and rodents has
demonstrated that familial cases can also be infec-

A comparison of affected siblings within a
family reveals a common age of death (plus or minus 6
months on average) but not a uniform date of death
(plus or minus 6 to 7 years on average), a disparity that
argues against simultaneous early exposure to an infec-
tious agent.26 The best evidence to date that the familial
forms of prion disease are inherited illnesses is derived
from experiments that show genetic linkage of a PrP
missense variant to the ataxic form of GSS.28
Genetic implications. In animals, an intricate rela-
tionship exists between the scrapie prion and the host. In mice, genetic data correlate PrP structure with host
susceptibility; the murine PrP gene was found to be
linked to susceptibility (ie, length of the incubation
time) for experimental s ~ r a p i e . ~ ~
Moreover, substitu-
tions of 2 amino acid residues at codons 108 and 189
correlate with short and long incubation times in ex-
perimental scrapie of mice.18 Further arguments for the
modulation of scrapie susceptibility, course of disease,
and neuropathology by PrP primary structure are de-
rived from the inoculation of transgenic mice express-
ing hamster PrP with hamster prions.3O Transgenic
mice inoculated with hamster prions developed scrapie
considerably earlier than control mice inoculated with
hamster prions and developed PrP plaques ordinarily
observed in hamsters but not in mice with scrapie. The chromosomal localization of human and murine
PrP genes appears to be homologous.

parallels the situation in mice with one important dif-

text:
In-
herited human prion diseases provide an opportunity to
examine how a disease can be, on the one hand, inher-
ited, and on the other, infectious. In particular, recent
studies of the genetics of familial prion diseases have
yielded 3 major results. First, significant genetic linkage
between ataxic GSS and PRNP indicates that this
horizontally transmissible disease is inherited through
a locus at or near PRNP.28 Second, a leucine substitu-
tion at PRNP codon 102 is genetically linked to ataxic
GSS in families from ethnically and lineally distinct
backgrounds, suggesting that this mutation arose inde-
pendently at least twice and is therefore more than a
linked genetic marker.28.32.33
Indeed, this substitution
may cause the disease or at least directly influence its
pathogenesis. Third, this and other mutations in PrP
found to track with disease in families with a variety of
prion diseases provide evidence for a strong but not
absolute correlation of specific mutations in PrP with
different clinical forms of familial prion disease^.^^.^^-^^
Studying how variations in PrP primary structure in-
fluence selective features of inherited prion diseases
may provide a window into the molecular mechanisms
of these neurodegenerative disorders. Clinical and pathologic aspects of inherited
prion diseases. Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinlzer
syndrome (GSS). In 1936, 2 neurologists, Gerstmann
and Straussler, and a neuropathologist, Scheinker, first
described a family with an autosomal dominant con-
dition that featured unusual plaques in the cerebellar
and cerebral hemispheres but otherwise resembled an
olivopontocerebellar atrophy with mild dementia.36
Named after its discoverers, this rare condition became
a focus of interest when, in 1981, it was shown to be
transmissible to experimental animals.27 The definition
of GSS has since grown to encompass a heterogeneous
group of neurodegenerative syndromes all bearing the
striking hallmark of multicentric PrP plaques in the
cerebellar and cerebral hemispheres.

source: Inherited human prion diseases (Hsiao, K. Prusiner, S. B.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
Unicentric kuru
plaques may also be present. The differential diagnosis
of GSS includes olivopontocerebellar atrophy, spino-
cerebellar degeneration, Wilson’s disease, multiple scle-
rosis, familial Alzheimer’s disease, metachromatic
leukodystrophy, abetalipoproteinemia (Bassen-Korn-
zweig syndrome), phytanic acid deficiency (Refsum’s
disease), intermittent porphyria, thyroid disease, and
Huntington’s chorea. Because the diagnosis of GSS is
based upon a neuropathologic feature, it cannot be
made in a given family without examining brain tissue
from an affected member. However, in the future the
molecular genetic correlates of inherited prion diseases
may facilitate premortem diagnosis and minimize the
need to obtain brain tissue. The average age of onset is 40 years, with a range from
age 19 to 66 years. The average duration of disease is 5
years with a range from 1 to 11 years. The age of onset
within a given family may vary by as much as 3 decades,
but usually falls within 2 decades. The exact incidence of
GSS is unknown, but as noted above, it is estimated to be
between 1 and 10 per hundred million. Most cases are
familial, but sporadic cases have been reported. Different types of GSS may be delineated on the
basis of clinical presentation. Since individuals within a
pedigree may exhibit variations in disease manifesta-
tions, the type of disease found in a pedigree is best
represented by a weighted composite of clinical presen-
tations from several affected members. The form of
disease originally described by Gerstmann, Straussler,
and Scheinker produced primarily ataxia and other
cerebellar signs, including gaze abnormalities. Pyra-
midal signs, such as spasticity, weakness, and Babinski
responses, were also present, as was a mild dementia. This form of GSS may be designated “ataxic GSS,”
since ataxia is the predominant feature of the disease in
most individuals.

text:
Pyra-
midal signs, such as spasticity, weakness, and Babinski
responses, were also present, as was a mild dementia. This form of GSS may be designated “ataxic GSS,”
since ataxia is the predominant feature of the disease in
most individuals. In other families with ataxic GSS,
inconstant signs such as seizures, myoclonus, amyotro-
phy, areflexia, and posterior column signs have also
been reported. Another form of GSS presents predominantly as
dementia with extrapyramidal and pyramidal signs,
designated “dementing GSS.” This form of GSS is best
represented in the English literature by family GCSA.37
In this family, pathologic findings were confined to the
telencephalon and diencephalon. So similar are the
clinical and pathologic features of this disease and Alz-
heimer’s disease that prior to the development of immu-
nohistologic methods for determining the composition
of amyloid plaq~es,l6.~~
the diagnosis of familial Alzhei-
mer’s disease was applied to this family. It is likely that
an Alsatian family, family And.,39 also has this form of
GSS. In these families, dementia, pyramidal,
pseudobulbar, and parkinsonian symptoms and signs
predominate. Some members of these families develop
ataxia, but it is usually a minor feature. One extended family, family BB, has an atypical
form of GSS characterized by ataxia, dementia, and
parkins~nism.~.~~

Jakob disease (CJD) refers to a heterogeneous group of
neurodegenerative conditions in which multicentric
GSS plaques are notably rare or absent, but in which a
disease-specific isoform of PrP, designated PrPSc, can
be found in immunoblots of brain homogenate~~~
or in
the form of unicentric PrP-positive kuru plaques. CJD
patients with and without kuru plaques differ in clinical
presentation. Most CJD patients without kuru plaques
present with dementia or other symptoms referable to
the cerebral cortex, such as visual or behavioral distur-
bances, whereas CJD patients with kuru plaques usu-
ally present with cerebellar symptoms.26
Five to 15% of CJD cases are familial. The average
age of death of patients with familial CJD in one series
was 51 years with a range of 20 to 73 years.26 The average
duration of disease was 11 months with a range of 1
month to 4 years.26
The molecular genetics of inherited prion dis-
eases. Four PrP variants have been shown to be genet-
ically linked to or track with inherited prion diseases
(figure, and table 2).

Four PrP variants have been shown to be genet-
ically linked to or track with inherited prion diseases
(figure, and table 2). Substitution of leucine for proline
at PrP codon 102 has been reported in 3 Caucasian and 2
Asian families with ataxic GSS.28,32,33,43 This substitu-
tion was not found in over 200 normal individuals and
patients with other neurologic illnesses, nor was it
found in patients with other forms of inherited prion
disease~.~8*3~*33,~3
Since this PrP variant is associated
with ataxic GSS from distinct ethnic backgrounds and
is not found in other forms of inherited prion diseases,
the codon 102 leucine variant possibly provokes multi-
centric plaque formation, and the cerebellum and cere-
bellar tracts may be more susceptible to degeneration
when this PrP variant is present. The codon 102 leucine variant is the only PrP muta-
tion that has been shown to be genetically linked to an
inherited prion disease. The mutation creates a Dde I
restriction site in the PrP open reading frame. Because
it involves the familiar CpG to TpG substitution,44
probably the result of deamination of a methylated
cytosine, de novo mutations are predicted. These would
appear as sporadic cases of ataxic GSS.& The leucine
variant would be expected to occur in 50% of offspring
unless the mutation were somatic or chimeric. Three other mutations have been found to track with

pedigrees involved preclude the attainment of statis-

perspective against the highly significant lod score (now

these mutations emanates from the following: (1) the 3
PrP point mutations are located in strictly conserved
regions of PrP when compared with 3 hamster species, 2
murine strains, rat and sheep PrP,18J9,46-48
and (2) the
mutant insert lies in a highly conserved region of PrP
comprised of octa-repeat sequences49 (L. Goldfarb, pre-
sented at Fondation pour l'Etude du Systhme Nerveux
Central et P6riph6rique: Regulation and Genetic Con-
trol of Brain Amyloid, New York, November 4, 1989). Substitution of valine for alanine at PrP codon 117 is
found in an American patient of German descent from
family GCSA with the dementing form of GSS with
pyramidal and parkinsonian features.34 This PrP vari-
ant has also been reported in an Alsatian patient from
family And. with a similar form of GSS exhibiting
dementia and pyramidal and pseudobulbar features.&
The codon 117 valine substitution probably arose as a
consequence of a CpG to TpG mutation in the 2nd
position of a silent alanine codon mutation (GCA to
GCG), which is found in 10% of normal Caucasians.5o
Both patients share a normal PrP variant involving
substitution of valine for methionine at codon 129.

Be-
cause 2 PrP variants are found in the putative disease
allele of both patients, it seems possible that these
patients shared a common European founder. The
codon 117 valine variant is probably not the only PrP
variant associated with the dementing form of GSS,
since it has not been found in a patient from an unre-
lated family (family Ant.). Complete sequences of the
PrP open reading frames from this patient are not yet
known. A 144-bp insert at PrP codon 53 is found in a British
family, family Per., with CJD35v49 (L. Goldfarb, ibid),
and substitution of lysine for glutamate at PrP codon
200 is found in 2 American families with CJD and in
Slovakian Czechs with CJD.33*51
Neither of these muta-
tions can be found in a Finnish CJD family, family S52
(K. Hsiao, unpublished observations). The complete
sequence of PrP open reading frames in this family is
not yet known. An insert is found at or near PrP codon
53 in another British patient with a familial neuro-
degenerative illness (see family B), but because neuro-
pathologic information from this family is not
available, a definitive clinicopathologic diagnosis has
not been made.53 This insert has also been found in a
family with a presenile dementia in which gliosis or
spongiform change characteristic for CJD was lack-
ing.54 A 96-bp insert at the same location is found in 1
patient with familial CJD (L. Goldfarb, ibid). Both the
96-bp and 144-bp inserts encode sequences comprised of
multiples of octa-repeat~~~
(L. Goldfarb, ibid). The
wild-type PrP gene contains 5 octa-repeats, and the
shorter and longer inserts encode an additional 4 octa-
repeats and 6 octa-repeats, respectively. It is interesting
to note that these inserts at codon 53 fall outside the
protease-resistant portion of PrPSc.

allelic frequency of 33 to 35% in Caucasians; homo-

Caucasians55 (S. DeArmond and L. Stowring, personal

valine variant.% These figures either represent sam-
pling error or they preliminarily suggest that individu-

more susceptible to prion diseases. None of the 4 known disease-associated PrP variants
is found in family BB with GSS and neurofibrillary
tangles. Complete sequence data of both PrP alleles in 3
patients from family BB revealed only a codon 129
valine variant in the open reading frame common to
these patients.57 No other mutation was found in the
PrP open reading frame, implying that the mutation
that causes disease in this family does not reside in the
PrP open reading frame. The striking numbers of
neurofibrillary tangles suggest that a parallel process
independent of prions may be involved. A mutation
elsewhere in the genome may influence the pathogene-
sis of both prions and neurofibrillary tangles.

December 1990 NEUROLOGY 40 1823
this family provides a heuristic link between the prion
diseases and such disorders as Alzheimer’s disease re-
mains to be established. It certainly seems possible that individuals in some
families with inborn errors of PrP metabolism will not
produce infectious prion particles. If this is the case,
then it will be important to distinguish between those
PrP mutations associated with infectious prions and
those in which transmission to experimental animals
cannot be demonstrated. Perhaps it will be necessary to
refer to “inherited human prion diseases,” denoting
those in which infectivity is present, and “inherited
human prion protein diseases,” denoting those in which
infectivity is absent but a mutant PrP is present. These
issues cannot be resolved at the present time, because
assays of infectivity are limited by the incomplete rate
of horizontal transmission across species barriers. Hopefully, this problem can be overcome through the
use of transgenic mice expressing human PrP genes.30
Phenotypic expression of PrP mutants in disease. The techniques of molecular biology may enable current
research to supplement and clarify the efforts of earlier
neurologists and neuropathologists in the classification
of the inherited prion diseases. Upon surveying the
available data, it now appears that families presenting
with specific clinical and pathologic features of inheri-
ted prion diseases will be found to fit within single
mutational classes (table 2). Conversely, by examining
families with inherited prion diseases within single mu-
tational classes, unifying clinical and pathologic fea-
tures may be identified.

source: Inherited human prion diseases (Hsiao, K. Prusiner, S. B.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
Conversely, by examining
families with inherited prion diseases within single mu-
tational classes, unifying clinical and pathologic fea-
tures may be identified. Eventually, this approach may
lead to the delineation of functional regions of PrP
involved in the pathogenesis of selected features of
prion diseases. Based upon currently known molecular
genetic information, the features of the inherited prion
diseases that are determined by the primary structure of
PrP appear to be (1) plaque formation and morphology;
(2) the topographic distribution of lesions, resulting in
distinct clinical presentations; and (3) host range. Role of PrP primary structure in amyloid plaque
formation. Studies of mice expressing a hamster PrP
transgene argue that the primary structure of PrP influ-
ences plaque formation. Transgenic mice inoculated
with hamster scrapie develop plaques in locations iden-
tical to those of hamsters with scrapie, whereas non-
transgenic littermates and other control mice
inoculated with hamster scrapie do not develop
plaques.3O Whether a region of PrP in the vicinity of
codon 102 is the “GSS plaque locus” is a tantalizing
possibility. This idea is supported by several additional
lines of circumstantial evidence: (1) the only other PrP
mutation associated with GSS thus far discovered is
nearby at codon 117; (2) codons 102 and 107 in hamster
PrP distinguish the plaque-forming Chinese and Syrian
hamsters from the non-plaque-forming Armenian
hamstep, and (3) as plaques were not observed in ei-
ther of the CJD faniilies studied, the location of the
known mutations outside the region putatively in-
volved in GSS plaque formation is consistent with the
notion of a GSS plaque locus in the vicinity of codon
102.

Whether PrP variants in CJD families with kuru
plaques segregate from PrP variants in CJD families
1824 NEUROLOGY 40 December 1990
without amyloid plaques is unknown, but would be
predicted if a plaque locus or loci in PrP exists. In long-incubation-period mice (Prn*), amyloid
plaque formation is not governed entirely by PrP pri-
mary structure; plaques have been reported to occur
following inoculation with a particular isolate or
“strain” of murine scrapie pri0n,5*,~~
but not with other
isolates. Whether PrP amyloid plaque formation in hu-
mans is governed entirely by the primary structure of
PrP or is dependent upon other factors remains to be
established. The role of PrP primary structure in topography of
lesions. There is a striking correlation of the codon 102
leucine variant with a predominantly cerebellar clinical
presentation, but the molecular basis for this to-
pographic specificity is not apparent. In transgenic
mice expressing hamster PrP the topography of lesions
parallels that normally found in hamsters, again sup-
porting the hypothesis that PrP primary structure in-
fluences the topography of lesions.3O However, genes
other than PRNP probably also modulate the topo-
graphic selectivity of lesions, as the variations of clini-
cal presentation within families would suggest. The role of PrP primary structure in determining
host range. The experimental transmission of prions to
heterologous hosts is invariably associated with a pro-
longed incubation period, and successful transmissions
frequently occur in only a minority of the inoculated
animals. This barrier between heterologous hosts was
first labeled the “species barrier” by Pattison.GO Trans-
mission of prions from humans into one experimental
host may not be achieved in another.

source: Inherited human prion diseases (Hsiao, K. Prusiner, S. B.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
This barrier between heterologous hosts was
first labeled the “species barrier” by Pattison.GO Trans-
mission of prions from humans into one experimental
host may not be achieved in another. In some cases
transmission of human CJD to nonhuman primates
was successful, but transmission to rodents or goats did
not occur.61
The molecular cloning and sequencing of PrP genes
from different species raised the possibility that the
species barrier or host range of prions was due to dif-
ferences in PrP sequence. Each species examined was
found to have a distinct incubation time as well as a
distinct PrP sequence. An experimental test of the hy-
pothesis that PrP sequence determined incubation time
involved constructing transgenic mice expressing
hamster PrP genes. Persuasive evidence arguing that
prion host range is determined by PrP primary struc-
ture resulted from these studies: a hamster PrP trans-
gene in mice rendered these mice susceptible to hamster
prion~.~O
Furthermore, both protease-resistant hamster
PrP and hamster prions were generated in the brains of
these scrapie-infected transgenic mice. The results with transgenic mice extended earlier
studies showing that species-specific epitopes of PrP
are host-determined. In those studies transmission of
human CJD prions into mice required prolonged in-
cubation times of more than 1 year whereas subsequent
passages in mice required about 120 days.12 Western
blotting studies demonstrated protease-resistant
human PrP in the human CJD inoculum but only
mouse PrP was found in subsequent prion inocula de-
rived from mice. Deciphering the precise molecular mechanisms in-
volved in transmission of prions between heterologous
hosts may prove to be a formidable task due to the
prolonged incubation times required for such transmis-
sions. Presumably, the host cellular PrP does not read-
ily recognize the inoculated PrP molecules.

source: Inherited human prion diseases (Hsiao, K. Prusiner, S. B.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
Deciphering the precise molecular mechanisms in-
volved in transmission of prions between heterologous
hosts may prove to be a formidable task due to the
prolonged incubation times required for such transmis-
sions. Presumably, the host cellular PrP does not read-
ily recognize the inoculated PrP molecules. Whether
this process involves a stochastic mechanism or addi-
tional factors besides PrP amino-acid sequence is un-
known. However, transgenic mouse experiments argue
that an interaction between host cellular PrP and PrP
in the prion inoculum must occur either during the
initiation or maintenance of scrapie infection. Whether differences in transmission of human GSS
prions to rodents from patients with the same mutation
reflects a stochastic process or additional factors in the
inoculum remains to be determined. Brain homoge-
nates from both patients tested in family CBWU pro-
duced neurologic disease in 13 of 13 hamsters, but brain
homogenates from 1 patient tested in family J did not
produce neurologic disease in any of 8 hamstemZ8 It
may be significant that codon 129 in the mutant PrP
allele in family CBWU encodes a valine, while in family
J it encodes a methionine. Further studies are required
to determine whether factors besides PrP primary
structure influence host range. Other phenotypic determinants in prion diseases. PrP primary structure appears to be an insufficient
determinant of several disease features including age of
onset and disease duration.

text:
Further studies are required
to determine whether factors besides PrP primary
structure influence host range. Other phenotypic determinants in prion diseases. PrP primary structure appears to be an insufficient
determinant of several disease features including age of
onset and disease duration. A comparison of the 2 white
families with ataxic GSS, families J and CBWU, in
which the initial linkage analysis of the codon 102 leu-
cine variant to ataxic GSS was performed reveals a 2-
decade difference between the age of onset in these
families and a 3-decade span in age of onset within
family CBWU itself.28.62.63
Since no specific differences
in PrP primary structure distinguish affected individu-
als within a family, the disparity in age of onset would
appear to depend upon factors besides PrP primary
structure. In family CBWU, disease duration ranged from 1 to
11 years.62.63 Since the PrP allele containing the codon
102 leucine variant tracks with disease in this family, it
is unlikely that this same allele can mediate differences
in disease duration. It is clear from studies of scrapie
incubation times in mice that other genetic loci acting
independently of the murine prion protein gene or gene
complex cause large variations in incubation times.64
Other genes are probably also involved in modulating
some prion disease phenotypes in humans. Epidemiologic considerations. A unifying explana-
tion for the pathogenesis of human prion diseases must
take their epidemiologic characteristics into considera-
tion. Human prion diseases manifest in 3 ways: they can
be infectious, as exemplified by kuru and accidental
CJD; they appear sporadically, as exemplified by CJD;
and they can be inherited, as in GSS and familial CJD.

text:
Human prion diseases manifest in 3 ways: they can
be infectious, as exemplified by kuru and accidental
CJD; they appear sporadically, as exemplified by CJD;
and they can be inherited, as in GSS and familial CJD. The transmissibility of prions in kuru and accidental
CJD illustrates their infectious nature, while the estab-
lishment of a causal relationship between germline mu-
tations in PrP and the development of inherited prion
diseases argues for a genetic mechanism. How prion synthesis is initiated in patients with
inherited prion diseases is unknown. Once prions are
present, the relative efficiency by which wild-type and
variant forms of PrP are recruited into the formation of
more prions is also unknown. The mechanism by which sporadic disease occurs is
unknown. Somatic mutations in PrP, recessive muta-
tions in PrP creating the appearance of sporadic dis-
ease, or exogenous infection of susceptible individuals
remain possibilities. Conclusion. A wide variety of independent disciplines
including protein chemistry, molecular genetics, immu-
nochemistry, neuropathology, and experimental neu-
rology have greatly strengthened the hypothesis that
the prion disease-specific isoform of PrP, PrPSe, plays a
central role in the etiology of human and animal prion
diseases. Whether prion particles are composed of a
small, as yet unidentified, molecule, such as a nucleic
acid tightly bound to PrPSe, or PrP& alone, is unknown.

source: Inherited human prion diseases (Hsiao, K. Prusiner, S. B.) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
Whether prion particles are composed of a
small, as yet unidentified, molecule, such as a nucleic
acid tightly bound to PrPSe, or PrP& alone, is unknown. The discovery of scrapie isolates or “strains” has been
used to argue for a nucleic acid genome within the
prion,65,= but numerous studies reviewed elsewhere
have failed to provide any evidence for such a macro-
m~lecule.~
Although recent studies argue persuasively
that PrP* is formed during a post-translational event
from PrPC, the cellular form of PrP found in normal and
diseased animals, or from a common precursor, the
molecular basis for this conversion remains to be estab-
l i ~ h e d . ~ ~
The appearance of disease-specific mutations
or sets of mutations in PrP strengthens the hypothesis
that a causal relationship exists between PrP and dis-
ease. Proof of this relationship would be achieved only
with the properly controlled demonstration of de novo
prion generation in cultured cells or animals containing
mutant PrP genes. The formal possibility that the PrP
gene is a susceptibility gene or its product is a receptor
for an environmental agent remains. However, because
different mutants are associated with different disease
phenotypes, a susceptibility or receptor mechanism
would have to involve either selective susceptibility to a
variety of ubiquitous environmental agents, or indis-
criminate susceptibility to 1 agent followed by a specific
influence of each mutation on different phenotypic as-
pects of disease. These putative environmental agents
have not been discovered; indeed, current knowledge
favors a direct role for PrP& in both the transmission
and pathogenesis of prion diseases. Addendum.
