SAF preparations have
the potential to yield a highly concentrated and puriﬁed form of PrPSc that
retains a signiﬁcant amount of infectivity. However, because the lipids have
been removed, the physicochemical properties of native PrPSc are not
maintained. The isolation of intact cells from infected brain tissue (14)
and the isolation of CLDs (68) produce two other distinct preparations
containing PrPSc. In the majority of the published clearance studies, researchers have
used either crude brain homogenates or microsomal preparations as their
spiking materials. For Bayer’s standard plasma process clearance studies,
crude brain homogenate prepared from hamsters infected with the 263K
strain of scrapie is used. Some researchers use more puriﬁed preparations
such as microsomal fractions because the PrPSc has been concentrated and
some of the brain tissue impurities have been removed. Regardless of
which material is used, care must be taken to ensure that the spiking
preparation does not signiﬁcantly interfere with the normal performance
of the scaled-down process simulation. Typically, this is controlled by
performing mock clearance studies in which the process simulation is
spiked with a sample of normal (i.e., not infected) brain homogenate that
has been prepared in the same manner as the infected spiking material. Process characterization tests are performed to determine whether this
mock spike aﬀects the performance of the scaled-down process. If the
mock spike interferes with the process, then a lower concentration of
spiking material may be necessary or the process cannot be assessed for
TSE removal. V. CLEARANCE RESULTS FOR BIOLOGICAL PRODUCTS
A. Bayer’s Plasma Fractionation Clearance Studies
The objectives of Bayer’s clearance studies were to determine how PrPSc
and TSE infectivity partition during the course of isolation of therapeutic
proteins from human plasma and to demonstrate the utility of PrPSc as a
marker for tracking TSE infectivity.

Bayer’s Plasma Fractionation Clearance Studies
The objectives of Bayer’s clearance studies were to determine how PrPSc
and TSE infectivity partition during the course of isolation of therapeutic
proteins from human plasma and to demonstrate the utility of PrPSc as a
marker for tracking TSE infectivity. Both animal bioassays and a PrPspeciﬁc Western blot assay were used to assess plasma fractionation processes for their ability to remove TSE infectivity and PrPSc from product
streams. For each process analyzed, a minimum of three independent
fractionations was performed, and each sample set was assessed at least
twice using the Western blot assay. Currently seven diﬀerent plasma fractionation processes have been examined (52). Each plasma intermediate
Miller et al.

used as the starting material for a speciﬁc process was spiked with crude
hamster scrapie brain homogenate containing a known amount of infectivity and PrPSc, and each fractionation step was performed independently
in the scaled-down format. Table 3 includes data from Bayer’s plasma
fractionation clearance studies using hamster scrapie as the spiking
material. The ﬁrst set of Bayer plasma protein fractionation processes examined
comprises the ‘‘Cohn trunk’’ of the human plasma protein puriﬁcation
process. These are the basic processes from which Bayer plasma proteins are
derived. The Cohn scheme of protein puriﬁcation is comprised of several
processing steps that involve various combinations of the following methods
to facilitate the precipitation of diﬀerent groups of proteins: (1) addition of
alcohol, (2) temperature adjustments, and (3) pH adjustments. As the ﬁrst step, cryoprecipitation is separate from the Cohn scheme
(Fig. 4). At this step, frozen pooled plasma is thawed and the precipitated
material is separated from the supernatant (eﬄuent). The resulting eﬄuent
is the starting solution for the next process in the Cohn trunk, the
fraction I separation.

As the ﬁrst step, cryoprecipitation is separate from the Cohn scheme
(Fig. 4). At this step, frozen pooled plasma is thawed and the precipitated
material is separated from the supernatant (eﬄuent). The resulting eﬄuent
is the starting solution for the next process in the Cohn trunk, the
fraction I separation. The eﬄuent produced from the fraction I separation
is the starting material for the fraction II+III separation, and so on
through the fraction IV-1 and fraction IV-4 separations (Fig. 4). Conventionally, clearance is deﬁned as the diﬀerence between the PrPSc or
infectivity detected in the prove sample and the product-containing
fraction, which is usually the eﬄuent. In these initial studies, the levels
of PrPSc/infectivity clearance were deﬁned as nominal (<2.0 logs), intermediate (2.0–4.0 logs), or substantial (>4.0 logs). Cryoprecipitation demonstrated nominal clearance for both PrPSc and infectivity with respect to the
eﬄuent. Fraction I also showed nominal clearance for PrPSc; however,
infectivity clearance was not measured. The fraction II+III and fraction
IV-4 separations each demonstrated substantial clearance. According to the
classiﬁcation scheme described above, the fraction IV-1 separation demonstrated substantial clearance for PrPSc and intermediate clearance for
infectivity. A second set of plasma processes was also examined. These puriﬁcation
steps are product-speciﬁc and branch oﬀof the primary Cohn puriﬁcation
scheme (Fig. 4). For the puriﬁcation of factor VIII a 3% polyethylene glycol
(PEG) precipitation is performed where initial cryoprecipitate paste is
resuspended and incubated with PEG. The resulting precipitate is discarded
and the eﬄuent is further processed to factor VIII. TSE partitioning studies
for this step demonstrated an intermediate clearance of PrPSc and TSE
infectivity with respect to factor VIII.

B. Plasma Fractionation Clearance Studies from
Other Groups
Three other research groups have published studies on prion partitioning
for plasma fractionation using Cohn-Oncley processes (Table 3). The
spiking materials used in all three studies were derived from hamster
scrapie brains (263K), but they were prepared and spiked using diﬀerent
methods. In the Brown et al. study (14), a trypsinized cellular fraction was
spiked into whole human blood. The plasma was collected from this
sample and used as the starting material for partitioning studies. Using the
animal bioassay, Brown and co-workers observed varying levels of TSE
infectivity clearance for four plasma fractionation steps (Table 3). Partitioning of PrPSc was not measured in this study. Foster and co-workers
used a microsomal preparation, and spiked a variety of plasma intermediates used in their Cohn-Oncley processes (66). They also examined
clearance in some ﬁltration and chromatography steps. Partitioning of
PrPSc was measured using a Western blot assay; however, TSE infectivity
was not measured (Table 3). Baron (69) compared four diﬀerent preparations of spiking materials that contained PrPSc in its least puriﬁed
form to a highly puriﬁed form. PrPSc partitioning was analyzed using
a conformation-dependent immunoassay, but TSE infectivity partitioning
was not evaluated. Despite the diﬀerences in the fractionation processes and the spiking
materials used in these studies, the trends for TSE infectivity and PrPSc
partitioning were similar. In general, the data from all three groups indicate
a progressive increase in clearance as the plasma fractionation processes
proceed toward the isolation of human albumin (Table 3 and Figure 4). This trend correlates well with the data from Bayer’s partitioning studies.

source: Prions and Mad Cow Disease (Brian K. Nunnally, Ira S. Krull) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
In general, the data from all three groups indicate
a progressive increase in clearance as the plasma fractionation processes
proceed toward the isolation of human albumin (Table 3 and Figure 4). This trend correlates well with the data from Bayer’s partitioning studies. There is also an indication that a greater amount of clearance is observed
when a highly puriﬁed form of PrPSc is used as the spiking material (69). However, it seems that a less puriﬁed spiking material such as crude
homogenate presents a greater challenge to the system and therefore may
represent a worst-case scenario for plasma fractionation clearance studies. C. Independent Plasma Fractionation Steps vs. a Series
of Coupled Steps
The majority of TSE clearance studies have been performed on isolated
plasma protein puriﬁcation steps. However, plasma manufacturing processes are normally performed as a puriﬁcation series where the fractionation product from one step is immediately processed through the subsequent
processing steps. Simply summing clearance from individual steps could
Miller et al.

potentially overestimate the total clearance value in relation to a speciﬁc
protein product, by ignoring the possibility that there could be PrPSc
populations that may be resistant to a particular partitioning mechanism. To address this question, clearance studies were performed in which a
sample of pooled plasma was spiked with SBH and ﬁve consecutive steps of
the plasma fractionation process were performed in a series. In this
experimental format, each step was coupled to the previous step, in that
the starting material for one step was produced from the previous step. Therefore, any PrPSc or infectivity that was not removed from the product
stream by one processing step would be available for partitioning in the
subsequent processing step.

source: Prions and Mad Cow Disease (Brian K. Nunnally, Ira S. Krull) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
Therefore, any PrPSc or infectivity that was not removed from the product
stream by one processing step would be available for partitioning in the
subsequent processing step. The steps examined in this series included cryoseparation, fraction I
separation, fraction II+III separation, fraction III separation, and fraction
IV-1 separation, which lead to the isolation of immunoglobulins, ATIII,
PPF, albumin, and a1-proteinase inhibitor (Fig. 4). Results indicated that
PrPSc and infectivity that was not removed by one fractionation step was
removed by a subsequent step (70). Also, the extent of the PrPSc and
infectivity clearance in the coupled fractionation was comparable to the
single step clearance observed previously (Table 3). This provided evidence
that a hypothetical, clearance-resistant population of PrPSc was not present, and that the removal of PrPSc by a series of processing steps can be
additive. A recent study suggests that the major factors that aﬀect PrPSc
partitioning in plasma fractionation steps include pH, salt content, and the
presence of ethanol (70). D. Clearance Studies for Biological Products That Are Not
Derived from Plasma
Although most of the TSE partitioning studies to date have been performed
on processes used for the production of therapeutics from human plasma,
some work has been done to address pathogen safety with respect to TSEs
for non-plasma-derived biological products, including recombinant proteins. For example, the production of Bayer’s recombinant factor VIII
provides an example of the numerous actions that manufacturers take to
reduce the risk of disease transmission by a recombinant product. The raw
materials and the manufacturing processes for producing recombinant
factor VIII have been carefully assessed for pathogen reduction and have
been designed to incorporate several methods for reducing potential pathogen safety risks.

source: Prions and Mad Cow Disease (Brian K. Nunnally, Ira S. Krull) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
The raw
materials and the manufacturing processes for producing recombinant
factor VIII have been carefully assessed for pathogen reduction and have
been designed to incorporate several methods for reducing potential pathogen safety risks. TSE spiking studies on process simulations have demonstrated that two of Bayer’s recombinant factor VIII chromatography steps
have the potential to remove TSE infectivity and PrPSc. Pathogen Safety of Biological Products

One of the earliest TSE clearance studies for biological products was
published by Golker and co-workers for aprotinin derived from bovine
lung tissue (71). In this study, the researchers used detergent-solubilized
brain homogenates obtained from a mouse-adapted strain of scrapie
(ME7) and measured infectivity by end-point titration. The researchers
analyzed four diﬀerent processing steps, one methanol extraction, two ionexchange chromatography steps, and a membrane ﬁltration step (Table 3). For every step analyzed, the authors reported a signiﬁcant level of TSE
infectivity clearance. E. Survey of Clearance Data
A survey of TSE clearance data for various biological therapeutic
proteins is provided in Table 3. Although various spiking agents and
preparations were used in these studies, only two analysis strategies were
employed: (1) measurement of the removal of the prion proteins or (2)
measurement of the removal of TSE infectivity. Some of the steps that
were analyzed were intentionally designed and/or implemented in manufacturing schemes for the sole purpose of pathogen removal. The most
notable of this particular group includes several ﬁltration steps. However,
the majority of manufacturing steps that were analyzed for their capacity
to clear TSEs were initially implemented for the purpose of isolating the
target protein. The fact that prions were removed from the product
stream was coincidental. A careful review of Table 3 reveals some patterns, especially for the
plasma precipitation steps.

source: Prions and Mad Cow Disease (Brian K. Nunnally, Ira S. Krull) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
The fact that prions were removed from the product
stream was coincidental. A careful review of Table 3 reveals some patterns, especially for the
plasma precipitation steps. Cryoprecipitation was performed by diﬀerent
groups using multiple assay methods and consistently resulted in V1 log of
clearance relative to the eﬄuent. The fractionation IV-1 and fractionation
IV-4 steps consistently demonstrated signiﬁcant TSE clearance for all
available data sets. The only apparent diﬀerence between Foster’s fraction
I+II+III (66) and Lee’s fraction II+III (52) precipitation steps was the
input material. The starting material for fraction I+II+III was cryopoor
(cryoprecipitated) plasma but the starting material for fraction II+III was
the fraction I eﬄuent, which was devoid of the fraction I and cryoprecipitate fractions. Therefore, the starting materials had slightly diﬀerent
milieus; however, the precipitation conditions for both of these steps were
equivalent (20% ethanol, pH 6.7, 5jC). The diﬀerences in starting
materials may account for the diﬀerent clearance values observed between
the two studies. Several ﬁltration studies are available for comparison. As expected,
the smaller pore membrane ﬁlters demonstrated some capacity to remove
prions. In fact, in the studies available for review, increasing clearance
Miller et al.

was observed as the membrane pore size decreased (72,73). In contrast,
the depth ﬁltrations described by Foster et al., which were associated
with puriﬁcation steps, appeared to be dependent on the ﬁlter pad/
support matrix that was used. Column chromatography using ionic mechanisms is becoming increasingly popular for biological product puriﬁcation at the production scale. Ion chromatography depends predominately
on the charge of the particle in solution, and the net charge of the protein depends on its isoelectric point and the buﬀer conditions. Owing to
the complex carbohydrates attached to the prion protein, a wide range
of isoelectric points has been reported for this protein (28).

source: Prions and Mad Cow Disease (Brian K. Nunnally, Ira S. Krull) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
Owing to
the complex carbohydrates attached to the prion protein, a wide range
of isoelectric points has been reported for this protein (28). Chromatographic methods are typically optimized during the process development
phase and are speciﬁcally designed for the recovery of the target protein,
not for prion removal. Because of the complexity of the prion protein’s
physicochemical nature, as well as the complexities of chromatographic
separations, general conclusions about the clearance potential of the prion
protein and/or TSE infectivity cannot be made and they must be determined
experimentally. VI. MODEL STUDIES
All of the clearance data described thus far were generated using spiking
materials derived from scrapie-infected rodents. Use of rodent models has
raised several concerns regarding its accuracy in predicting the partitioning
of TSE agents from other species, speciﬁcally humans. A number of
diﬀerences between mammalian TSE agents have been identiﬁed, including
species selectivity or species barrier, the primary sequence of the prion
protein, and other unidentiﬁed factors involved in infectivity and prion
replication (74). For instance, despite a high degree of prion sequence
homology at the amino acid level across mammalian species (75), small
changes in amino acid sequences may alter the physicochemical characteristics of the prion protein between species. These characteristics could
inﬂuence the partitioning of a particular species’ prion protein and the
associated infectivity. To determine whether the hamster 263K strain is an accurate model
for predicting the clearance of human TSEs, partitioning of the pathogenic
form of the prion protein associated with human variant CJD (PrPvCJD),
sporadic CJD (PrPsCJD), and Gerstmann Stra¨ ussler Sheinker disease
(PrPGSS) was measured in three plasma puriﬁcation processes (76). Because
sheep containing human transgenes may become an important future
source of biopharmaceuticals, a brain homogenate from scrapie-infected
sheep was tested also.

text:
Because
sheep containing human transgenes may become an important future
source of biopharmaceuticals, a brain homogenate from scrapie-infected
sheep was tested also. For these studies, the cryoseparation, 3% PEG, and
Pathogen Safety of Biological Products

11% PEG steps were analyzed (Fig. 4). The appropriate plasma intermediates were spiked with brain homogenates from patient samples or infected
sheep, and the partitioning of PrPvCJD, PrPsCJD, PrPGSS, and sheep PrPSc
was measured using Western blot assays (76). Regardless of whether
partitioning was nominal, intermediate, or substantial, the relative partitioning of human and sheep prions was consistent with the partitioning of
hamster PrPSc. Although small diﬀerences in the primary structure may change the
higher-order structure of the prion protein, these results demonstrate that
ﬁve diﬀerent strains of prion protein partition in a similar manner during
plasma fractionation processes. This indicates that the diﬀerences between
hamster, sheep, and human prion isoforms do not signiﬁcantly inﬂuence
PrP clearance in these processes, and that hamster PrPSc can be used to
reliably predict the partitioning of both human and sheep prion protein. Also, because there is a well-established correlation between the clearance
of hamster PrPSc and the clearance of hamster infectivity , it is reasonable to
conclude that human and sheep infectivity will partition similarly to
hamster infectivity. VII. SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS
Plasma and biotechnology product manufacturing provides for a means to
remove pathogens as a result of fractionation and puriﬁcation processes,
resulting in a reduced risk for the transmission of genuine or theoretical
pathogens. The demonstration that viral pathogens are inactivated or
removed during manufacturing provides a signiﬁcant margin of safety for
plasma-derived or biotech products. Therefore, demonstrating the potential
for plasma or biotech manufacturing processes to remove PrPSc/TSE
infectivity establishes an empirically determined margin of safety for this
theoretical risk.

source: Prions and Mad Cow Disease (Brian K. Nunnally, Ira S. Krull) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
The demonstration that viral pathogens are inactivated or
removed during manufacturing provides a signiﬁcant margin of safety for
plasma-derived or biotech products. Therefore, demonstrating the potential
for plasma or biotech manufacturing processes to remove PrPSc/TSE
infectivity establishes an empirically determined margin of safety for this
theoretical risk. In Bayer Corporation’s studies, the identiﬁcation of individual process
steps capable of eﬀective (4 logs or greater) and reproducible removal of
PrPSc/TSE infectivity from the many process steps involved in plasma
product manufacture required the development of a rapid in vitro assay
to detect PrPSc. Although the assay speciﬁcally detects the presence of PrPSc,
digestion with proteinase K to eliminate PrPc results in a banding pattern on
the Western blot characteristic of PrPRES. Quantitation using end-point
dilution analysis applied to the Western blot assay was selected because the
characteristic PrPRES banding pattern provides assurance that the signal is
due to the presence of PrPSc. However, any in vitro assay that speciﬁcally
detects PrPSc could be used for this application. The Western blot assay
Miller et al.

proved to be reproducible and quantitative over a 6-log dynamic range. Partitioning could be determined by spiking a scaled-down process step with
PrPSc and tracking it throughout the process. In most cases, PrPSc was
removed from the process because it partitioned into a fraction that was
eliminated from downstream manufacturing processes. Process steps capable of eﬀective PrPSc partitioning could be identiﬁed in several weeks as
opposed to many months or up to a year with the bioassay. However, it was
important to demonstrate that the PrPSc partitioning determined by Western blot correlated with TSE infectivity partitioning determined by bioassay. The results of comparative partitioning studies showed a strong correlation
between the partitioning of PrPSc determined by Western blot and TSE
infectivity determined by bioassay.

However, it was
important to demonstrate that the PrPSc partitioning determined by Western blot correlated with TSE infectivity partitioning determined by bioassay. The results of comparative partitioning studies showed a strong correlation
between the partitioning of PrPSc determined by Western blot and TSE
infectivity determined by bioassay. These results support the application of
a PrPSc in vitro assay as a predictor of TSE infectivity partitioning during
plasma or biotechnology fractionation and puriﬁcation steps. When applied
to the evaluation of PrPSc partitioning as a result of fractionation or
puriﬁcation, the assay identiﬁed individual process steps capable of partitioning 1 to >5 logs. If PrPSc/TSE infectivity were present in plasma, partitioning would
occur over the entire process. Therefore, in addition to identifying individual process steps capable of PrPSc partitioning, it was important to
demonstrate that PrPSc spiked into plasma could be removed by a series of
process steps. Several important questions concerning spiking and partitioning experiments were addressed by the studies reported here. Removal
was additive over the coupled process steps examined, demonstrating
that PrPSc that was not removed by one process step could be removed
by another, and conﬁrming that the addition of individual process steps
could predict the overall capacity of a manufacturing process to reduce
PrPSc load. Owing to the heterogeneous nature of PrPSc preparations,
there was a concern that a fraction of PrPSc may be resistant to removal. However, these studies showed that no fraction of the PrPSc spike was
found to be resistant to removal by precipitation/centrifugation, and the
removal of PrPSc by precipitation/centrifugation was independent of the
brain homogenate preparation used as the spiking material. This result was
consistent with experiments showing that precipitation/centrifugation is an
eﬃcient means of removing PrPSc regardless of whether the spiking
material was brain homogenate or puriﬁed PrPSc.

This result was
consistent with experiments showing that precipitation/centrifugation is an
eﬃcient means of removing PrPSc regardless of whether the spiking
material was brain homogenate or puriﬁed PrPSc. To date, published studies have investigated the partitioning and
removal of rodent-adapted TSE infectivity and PrPSc either as an endogenous component of blood or as spiked brain homogenates. Regardless of
whether the scaled-down process steps were conducted with endogenous
TSE infectivity from the blood of infected animals or homogenates of
infected brain, the results demonstrate that plasma fractionation processes
Pathogen Safety of Biological Products

have a signiﬁcant potential to remove PrPSc/TSE infectivity. This comparison
suggests that partitioning and removal of PrPSc/TSE infectivity determined
by spiking studies is similar to the removal of endogenous TSE infectivity
from the blood of infected animals. Of primary interest is the potential for plasma and biotechnology
manufacturing processes to remove the human forms of TSE. Owing to the
biochemical similarities between animal and human PrP/infectivity, both
species of PrPSc could be expected to partition in the same way during
fractionation or puriﬁcation. Nonetheless, it was important to demonstrate
that the partitioning of animal PrPSc and human PrPCJD was similar. The
results of the studies summarized here demonstrate that hamster PrPSc,
sheep PrPSc, and human PrPsCJD, PrPvCJD, and PrPGSS all partition in a
similar manner regardless of the partitioning step. Therefore, precipitation/
centrifugation spiking studies conducted with rodent-adapted PrPSc are
predictive of the partitioning and removal of human PrPCJD. Because we
have demonstrated that PrPSc partitioning correlates with TSE infectivity
partitioning, it also follows that rodent-adapted TSE infectivity partitioning
will be predictive of human CJD infectivity partitioning.

predictive of the partitioning and removal of human PrPCJD. Because we

partitioning, it also follows that rodent-adapted TSE infectivity partitioning
will be predictive of human CJD infectivity partitioning. The studies discussed here demonstrate the utility and relevance of
applying in vitro assays for the detection of PrPSc/CJD to identify plasma
and biotechnology manufacturing process steps that are capable of removing animal and human PrPSc/CJD. The PrPSc/CJD assay provides a practical

Clinical

Prions as a Cause of Infectious, Genetic, and Sporadic
Neurodegenerative
Diseases
Jeannie T. Lee, M.D., Ph.D. Depar-
of Pathology
Massachusetts General Hospital
Harvard Medical School
Boston, MA 02114
Introduction
Since Creutzfeldt described the fist
case of human spongiform enceph-
alopathy in 1920 (l), diseases caused
by what we now know as “prions” have
been a subject of considerable curiosity
and speculation. These diseases today
remain almost as diagnostically tanta-
lizing and therapeutically remote as
when they were first recognized as a
disease of chronic wasting and progres-
sive motor degeneration. Today, we de-
fine pi-ion diseases as a group of
unifomly fatal neurodegenerative dis-
eases affecting both humans and domes-
ticated animals (Table 1) (2). In
humans, they include Creutzfeldt-Jakob
disease (CID), Kuru, Gerstmann-
StrausslerScheinker
syndrome (GSS),
and fatal familial insomnia (FFI), and
have occurred throughout the world as
infectious, familial, and sporadic forms. In animals, various syndromes with re-
lated clinical and pathological features
have also been described, including
scrapie found in sheep worldwide,
chronic wasting disease of captive
mule deer and elk in North America,
and bovine spongiform encephalopathy
(BSE), which occurs primarily although
not exclusively in the British Isles. Prion diseases have attracted much
worldwide attention because of con-
cerns raised by conventional agricul-
tural and medical practices. The first
cases of BSE occurred in 1986 in Great
Britain among dairy and beef cattle, and
since that time, over 100,000 cattle
have succumbed (3). There are numer-
ous theories to explain the sudden ap-
pearance of a disease that had
previously been described only in hu-
mans, sheep, mink, and deer.

source: Prions as a cause of infectious, genetic, and sporadic neurodegenerative diseases (Jeannie T. Lee) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
There are numer-
ous theories to explain the sudden ap-
pearance of a disease that had
previously been described only in hu-
mans, sheep, mink, and deer. Some be-
lieved that ingestion of infected sheep
offal as dietary supplementation may
have been responsible for BSE (3), and
furthermore, that the mechanisms re-
sponsible for transmission of prions to
cattle may put humans at risk for infec-
tion following ingestion of infected cat-
tle products. Importantly, to date, no
anecdotal claims of animal transmission
to humans have ever been substanti-
ated, but human-to-human transmission
has occurred throughout the world. In
the United States, Japan, and Europe, ia-
trogenic introduction of CJD has re-
sulted from infected comeal grafts, dura
mater transplantation, neurosurgical in-
strumentation without proper steriliza-
tion, and use of growth hormone and
gonadotropins extracted from infected
human pituitary (4). These unfortunate
circumstances have brought caution to
the use of human brain tissue and de-
rivatives in therapy. The advent of molecular and cellular
biology has allowed for careful elucida-
tion of prion structure and pathogenesis
and is paving the way for improved di-
agnosis and prevention of disease. What we had previously referred to as
the “prion particle” is not a long-sus-
pected “slow virus” but is rather a sin-
gle aberrant protein with two surprising
features: first, it has a nearly identical
cellular counterpart; and second, it is de-
void of nucleic acids (5). The term
“prion” was introduced by Stanley Pru-
siner of the University of California,
San Francisco (U.C.F.S.) to distinguish
the etiologic agent from conventional
viruses and to emphasize its dual
pr-oteinaceous and vir-ion nature. This article will review our current
understanding of prion disease, the
mechanism of prion pathogenesis, and
application to clinical medicine.

various syndromes ranging from CID
to GSS (6). Patients with Creutzfeldt-
Jakob disease typically present acutely
with a rapidly progressive dementia ac-
companied by pyramidal and ex-
trapyrarnidal signs, such as ataxia and
spasticity. Death from intercurrent in-
fection and malnutrition usually ensues
within 6 mo of diagnosis, and autopsy
reveals spongiform changes in the cen-
tral nervous system with variable de-
gree of gliosis, the process of scar
formation by proliferating astrocytes re-
placing the neighboring degenerating
neurons. Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker syn-
drome, first described in 1936 by the
three physicians from whom the disease
name was derived, is a familial prion
disorder with a lengthier but equally fa-
tal course.

Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker syn-
drome, first described in 1936 by the
three physicians from whom the disease
name was derived, is a familial prion
disorder with a lengthier but equally fa-
tal course. Besides ataxia, spasticity,
and dementia, GSS patients often have
pseudobulbar symptoms such as speech
and swallowing difficulties. Although
spongiforrn degeneration and gliosis of
the brain are also present in GSS, amy-
loid plaque formation containing prion
protein is the predominant feature in vir-
tually all cases. Kuru is the third manifestation of hu-
man prion disease and was confined al-
most exclusively to the natives of
Papua New Guinea Once the most com-
mon cause of death among women and
children, km-u was characterized by
cerebellar ataxia, tremor, and wasting,
and had been traced to the practice of
ritualistic cannibalism that dictated the
ingestion of human brain matter. Death
follows within months after diagnosis,
and the kuru histopathology includes
variable degrees of spongiform neuro-
nal degeneration; about 70% of patients
show amyloid plaque formation (most
prominently in the cerebellum). Other human encephalopathies
thought to have prion origins include
fatal familiar insomnia and a number of
other atypical dementias currently un-
der investigation. Diagnosis and Transmission
Listed in Table 2 are several criteria
that have been recommended for the
diagnosis of human prion disease (6). Prion disease is suspected in any patient
who develops a progressive subacute or
chronic decline in cognitive and motor
function as elicited in the clinical his-
tory. Some argue that spongiform
changes be made the major diagnostic
criterion; however, it is important to em-
phasize that this is not an invariable fea-
ture of any of the disorders described
above.

Biology of the Prion
Protein
Although prion disease remains
therapeutically elusive, our under-
standing of its disease process has sig-
nificantly improved over the past
decade. The revelation that the prion
particle is a single aberrant protein that
can replicate without nucleic acids and
produce disease in much the same way
as viruses and bacteria has formed the
basis of a new biological paradigm for
the nature of microbial organisms and
their mechanisms of pathogenesis. The elucidation of prion biology
came after a series of intriguing find-
ings. In the 198Os, Stanley Prusiner and
colleagues (7,8) at U.C.S.F. purified
from scrapie-infected hamster brains a
protein of 27 to 30 kDa molecular
weight that is capable of transferring
disease to normal hamsters. This scra-
pie prion protein, or “PrP-sc,” was
shown to be devoid of nucleic acids, be-
cause treatment with DNA- and RNA-
damaging agents such as UV and
ionizing radiation, nuckases, and
psoralen do not reduce the infectivity of
the PrP-SC fraction. The protein was
also shown to be highly resistant to di-
gestion by a number of proteases, in-
cluding trypsin and SV-8, and can be
digested by proteinase K only with pro-
longed incubation under denaturing con-
ditions. On the basis of these
observations, Prusiner and colleagues
departed from conventional thinking
and proposed that the infectious agent
is a single protease-resistant protein
containing no nucleic acids at its core. Determination of its amino acid se-
quence enabled the synthesis of degen-
erate oligonucleotides for the
identification of cDNAs from infected
rodent expression libraries (9,10).

Both isoforms traverse the Golgi ap-
paratus where asparagine-linked oli-
gosaccharides are modified and further
modifications are made (5). PrP-c is
then transported to the external plasma
membrane by secretary vesicles. Some
stay anchored to the membrane by a
GPI moiety and a fraction is secreted
into the extracellular milieu. In contrast,
PrP-sc accumulates in cytoplasmic ves-
icles and gives rise to the “spongiform”
appearance of infected neurons on his-
tologic section. Although biophysical and biochemi-
cal studies show that the pi-ion protein
isoforms differ in conformation, the
question of whar initiates the conforma-
tional conversion and hence how the
disease process initiates remain intrigu-
ing in light of the fact that the primary
nucleic acid and amino acid sequences
are identical. In this regard, animal mod-
els have been instrumental in delineat-
ing potential mechanisms of disease. Early failures at achieving cross-spe-
cies infectivity led to the idea of a “spe-
cies barrier” ($15). Transmission of
hamster scrapie to mice by direct inocu-
lation into mouse brain was difficult,
and whenever successful, required long
incubation periods (16-18). However,
once disease develops in mice, inocu-
lum taken from infected mice produces
disease in subsequent passages in a ho-
mologous host with progressively
shorter incubation periods (Table 3). This suggests that sequential passage of
disease results in qualitative changes to
the priori protein that ease the induction
of disease. In transgenic mice expressing ham-
ster PrP, transmission of hamster scra-
pie is greatly facilitated (17,18), and
transgenic mice expressing a hybrid
PrP with sequences derived from ham-
ster and mouse have susceptibilities
that are intermediate (19). These studies
together argue that the relative suscepti-
bilities of animals to infection depend
on the degree of homology between the
infectious prion protein and the endo-
genous cellular protein (Table 3).

These studies
together argue that the relative suscepti-
bilities of animals to infection depend
on the degree of homology between the
infectious prion protein and the endo-
genous cellular protein (Table 3). Inter-
estingly, mice that do not express PrP-c
are resistant to prion disease (20), thus
indicating that propagation of prions de-
pends absolutely on preexisting expres-
sion of cellular prion protein. Based on results of animal studies
and on known structural differences be-
tween PrP-c and PrP-sc, a mechanism
for priori replication was proposed that
reconciles the pi-ion’s ability to cause
disease by infectious, genetic, and spo-
radic routes (11) (Figure 2). PrP-c is the
normal cellular protein for which sto-
chastic fluctuations can produce a con-
formation PrP-i, that is, intermediate
between PrP-c and the aberrant form
PrP-sc (kl). PrP-i can then convert into
PrP-SC in a second conformation change
(kz). In a normal cell, these conforma-
tion conversions occur at very low rates
(ki and kz), and insignificant quantities
of PrP-i and PrP-sc accumulate. How-
ever, the conformation changes can oc-
cur at an accelerated rate (k3) by the
presence of PrP-SC, which has autocata-
lytic activity in this model. According to the model, familial
forms of pi-ion disease result from muta-
tions in the prion protein that increase
the rate of conversion from PrP-c to
PrP-i, or alternatively, from PrP-i to
PrP-sc. In support of this hypothesis, 10
of 11 point mutations recognized in the
heritable disease lie within regions of
the protein believed to be important for

introduction of the mutation at codon
102 found in GSS into mice leads to the
development of spongiform degenera-
tion and gliosis similar to that found in
human disease (21). Infectious forms of
prion disease are postulated to result
from introduction of preformed PrP-SC,
which upon contact with the normal cel-
lular PrP-c initiates a series of autocata-
lytic chain reactions converting a
significant fraction of PrP-c to the aber-
rant PIP-SC. And finally, sporadic forms
can be explained by two mechanisms:
in the first possibility, the stochastic
process that converts PrP-c to PrP-i and
PrP-sc in the absence of any predispos-
ing factors operates in the unfortunate
individual to produce disease. In the
second scenario, a somatic mutation oc-
curs early in the life of the individual
that accelerates the production of PrP-
sc from PrP-c and PrP-i. Thus, to summarize the salient fea-
tures of the Prion Hypothesis: (i) The
prion agent is a single protein devoid of
nuclei acids (PrP-sc); (ii) The PrP-sc is
a product of abnormal folding of nor-
mal cellular prion protein (PrP-c), and
this aberrant form is highly resistant to
protease digestion; (iii) upon introduc-
tion into normal cells, PrP-sc can in-
duce conformational change in PrP-c. The efficiency of conversion is a func-
tion of the degree of homology between
the pathogenic PIP-SC and the endo-
genous PrPc. This conversion occurs
in a chain reaction leading to accumula-
tion of the aberrant protein over time. Thus, “replication” of the scrapie agent
is a conformational conversion event
that depends absolutely on the presence
of a continuous supply of cellular priori
protein.

There is currently no definitive test
for diagnosing prion disease, and until
recently, the diagnosis could be made
only by clinical evaluation and his-
tologic analysis of brain tissue. Elucida-
tion of prion molecular pathogenesis
has paved the way for more specific
testing using immunologic and molecu-
lar genetic techniques (22). A specific
diagnosis of prion disease can be made
by detection of the protease-resistant
isoform of prion protein. Several tech-

to detect aberrant PrP in patients with

antibodies directed against PrP will rec-
ognize PrP-c and PrP-SC equally well,
an extra proteinase K treatment step is
used to distinguish the relatively resis-

technique, requiring as little as 0.3 mg
of brain tissue for detection in CJD pa-

Im-
munoblotting is a sensitive and specific
technique, requiring as little as 0.3 mg
of brain tissue for detection in CJD pa-
tients. The limitation of this protocol is
that PrP-sc is not always detectable, par-
ticularly in patients with inherited prion
disease in whom PrP-sc levels may be
relatively low in early disease and in
cases where the prion particles show
variable geographic distribution within
the brain. As part of an effort to in-
crease the sensitivity of detection, Ser-
ban et al. (25) found that denaturation
of PrP-SC following proteinase K diges-
tion can significantly enhance the im-
munoreactivity of PrP-sc. This
technique allowed detection in 10 of 10
patients with a clinically and histologi-
cally confiied
diagnosis of CJD and
in one patient with GSS. Further testing
is required to evaluate the clinical util-
ity of this protocol. There is currently much interest in
adapting these protocols for use in less
invasive procedures, particularly for se-
rologic and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
testing. It remains to be determined
whether the concentration of PrP-sc in
body fluids is high enough to yield the
sensitivity required of diagnostic tests. For genetic forms of prion disease,
the diagnosis can be made by using
DNA extracted from peripheral blood
leukocytes at any stage of disease (15). These molecular genetic tests can also
be performed in genetic counseling and
prenatal diagnosis. Identification of mu-
tations cosegregating with affected indi-
viduals within the kindred is required to
make the diagnosis. To date, mutations
have been identified for all affected
families with clinical and histologic evi-
dence of prion disease (15,22). Point
mutations at codons 102 (P -_) L), 117

be emphasized, however, that since non-
pathogenic variations in PrP sequence
(DNA polymorphisms) also exist for
the human PrP gene, caution is required
in making the diagnosis based on ge-
netic criteria. Furthermore, while ge-
netic testing is powerful for diagnosing
familial prion disease, it is rarely of util-
ity in sporadic and infectious priori dis-
eases. In summary, no single laboratory
test alone will unfailingly and defini-
tively diagnose prion disease. Neverthe-
less, although today one still relies a
good part on clinical suspicion and
pathologic examination, neurologists
are increasingly relying on adjunctive
molecular and immunologic techniques. Currently, a positive test on (i) immuno-
histochemical staining of histologic sec-
tions, (ii) immunoblotting of brain
homogenate, and/or (iii) mutational
analysis of the PrP gene are strong indi-
cators of prion disease. It is, in fact, rec-
ommended that a diagnosis of priori
disease should not be ruled out in pa-
tients with atypical neurodegenerative
signs until at least one of these new
tests is performed. Summary: Prion Analogues in
Other Organisms? The priori hypothesis represents sig-
nificant departure from conventional
biological paradigm. It rests on the
premise that a single molecule can be
pathogenic and can be “infectious” by
recruiting preformed normal cellular
proteins, so that in effect, the “patho-
gen” can propagate itself without any
nucleic acid template. This provocative
hypothesis is borne out by a wealth of
animal models and in vitro biochemical
studies.

source: Prions as a cause of infectious, genetic, and sporadic neurodegenerative diseases (Jeannie T. Lee) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
This provocative
hypothesis is borne out by a wealth of
animal models and in vitro biochemical
studies. There is even evidence that sin-
gle-celled organisms possess priori ana-
logues. Wickner (26) has observed that,
in Saccharomyces
cerevisiae, a protein
involved in metabolizing nitrogenous
compounds called “Ure2p” can sponta-
neously convert into an aberrant confor-
mational isoform called “Ure3.”
Although Ure3 does not apparently
compromise yeast survival in a way
that PrP-sc does in humans and ani-
mals, it has catalytic potential to con-
vert other Ure2p into the inactive Ure3
isoform. The discovery of prion-type behav-
ior in other proteins and in other organ-
isms not only lends credence to
Prusiner’s hypothesis, but also suggests
that the priori mechanism may be more
widespread in nature than originally sus-
pected. It will be interesting to see what
other human diseases of “idiopathic”
origin can be explained by a similar
mechanism. References

The clinicopathological spectrum of Creutzfeldt-
Jakob disease has recently been extended by the
identification of an apparently new variant of this
disorder in the UK. The hypothesis that this new
disorder is causally related to the transmissible
agent
responsible
for
bovine
spongiform
encephalopathy has prompted re-evaluation of the
relationships between human and animal transmis-
sible spongiform encephalopathies, and reinforced
the need for adequate experimental models to
investigate this field. Recent experimental trans-
mission studies of bovine spongiform encephalopa-
thy into primates have supported the hypothesis,
and reinforced the central role of neuropathology in
the investigation of this group of diseases. Whilst
clearly of distinctive etiology, Creutzfeldt-Jakob dis-
ease shares both clinical and neuropathological fea-
tures with other human dementias; renewed evalu-
ation of potentially similar disease mechanisms in
these devastating conditions might provide new
information of both scientific and therapeutic value. Introduction
Over the past few months, there has been intense
medical, scientific and public interest in Creutzfeldt-
Jakob disease (CJD) following the identification of
an apparently new variant of this disorder ( vCJD) in
the UK (83). This unprecedented interest has
prompted renewed evaluation of the transmissible
spongiform encephalopathies (TSE) in man with ref-
erence to their relationship with similar disorders in
animals (38), particularly bovine spongiform
encephalopathy (BSE) (801, to disease pathogenesis,
and to diagnosis and relationship with other neu-
rodegenerative disorders. These considerations must
in turn be set within the context of current informa-
tion on the molecular biology and genetics of ani-

The concept of CJD as a clinical and pathological
entity has evolved considerably from the initial
descriptions by Creutzfeldt and Jakob in the 1920s
(33, 46). The history of the clarification of the clini-
cal and pathological features of this disease has
recently been reviewed by Richardson and Masters
(74); the recognition of CJD as a distinct disease enti-
ty was considerably advanced by the demonstration
of transmissibility to other species in 1967 (40). Subsequent advances in the study of the pathology
and clinical features of this disease have enabled CJD
to be sub-classified according to etiology (Table 1). This disease occurs most commonly as a sporadic dis-
order (6,17,81), although it could be argued that the
term idiopathic rather than sporadic is preferable,
since the cause of this form of CJD, with its remark-
ably consistent world-wide incidence at around 1 per
million population per annum (17, 36, Sl), is
unknown. The majority of sporadic CJD cases can be
identified clinically according to standard criteria
first devised by Masters et al. (59) and subsequently
modified in light of information on the molecular
genetics of human TSE and the identification of pro-
tease-resistant prion protein (PrPres) accumulation in
the brain (82).

Numerous eponymous clinical variants of sporadic
CJD have long been recognized (6, 59, 74), although
recent prospective CJD surveillance studies have
found that the boundaries between these clinical
subgroups are frequently ill-defined (77, 82). Most
cases of CJD occur in adults aged 60-65, although it
has been recognized for many years that a wide age
range can be affected, from teenagers to patients in
their ninth decade (10,16,19, 53, 64, 67, 82). The UK
CJD Surveillance Project has found in recent years an
apparently increasing number of CJD cases in indi-
viduals aged 75 and over, which appears to be a con-
sequence of increased diagnostic vigilance in the
elderly (76, 82). Most patients have a disease dura-
tion of six months or less, although cases with a pro-
longed disease duration over several years have been
described in the past (22, SO). The most common
clinical presentation is a rapidly progressive demen-
tia, subsequently accompanied by myoclonus or
other movement disorders, with cortical blindness
and akinetic mutism occurring later in the disease
(6, 15, 19, 82). However, a significant sub-popula-
tion of sporadic CJD patients presents with a progres-
sive cerebellar syndrome and subsequently develops
dementia (19, 20, 82); this clinical pattern is also
predominant in cases of iatrogenic CJD associated
with human growth hormone (hGH) therapy (11,
21). Electroencephalography (EEG) studies in spo-
radic CJD show a characteristic triphasic abnormality
with periodic sharp wave complexes in around 60-
70% of cases (13, 19). This finding is frequently tran-
sient and may occur occasionally in other neurode-
generative disorders (82). The pathophysiological
basis for this abnormality is uncertain, although it is
tempting to speculate that it might be a consequence
of disruption of the postulated role for the normal
cellular isoform of prion protein in synaptic function

also emphasized phenotypic variation; the areas of
the brain involved by spongiform change, astrocyto-
sis and neuronal loss are enormously variable from
case to case; within an individual case there is often
considerable variability of these features between
anatomical regions, requiring extensive histological
sampling for diagnosis and assessment (9, 24, 54). Recent attempts have been made to quantify these
differences using a computer-based image analysis
system; this technique has been used to quantitate
successfully both spongiform change and astrocytosis
(56, 75), and will undoubtedly be of continuing
importance as a tool in the study of this disease. The
remaining classical histopathological feature, the
amyloid plaque, has also been recognized to be a
variable finding in CJD. In sporadic CJD, amyloid
plaques occur in around 10% of cases (6, 9, 52) in
association with one or more valine alleles at codon
129 in the prion protein gene (PRNP) (33), and are
found most frequently in the cerebellum as rounded
fibrillary structures which are usually situated in the
granular cell or molecular layer, resembling the
plaques first identified in kuru (51) (Figure 1). Similar plaques occur at increased frequencies and
with a more widespread distribution in hGH iatro-
genic CJD cases (ll), and in certain familial forms of
CJD associated with mutations in the PRNP (3, 41,
49).

The CJD Surveillance Unit in the UK recently
reported a new variant of CJD which had occurred in
10 young patients (median age 29 years) with a pro-
longed disease duration (median 12 months) (83). The two youngest patients ( aged 16 and 18 years at
disease onset) had previously been reported (7,14). The clinical features in all 10 patients were similar,
including a psychiatric presentation often accompa-
nied by sensory abnormalities. Cerebellar signs and
symptoms developed subsequently, followed by
myoclonus and other movement disorders. Dementia
usually occured at a late stage, often with cortical
blindness and akinetic mutism. EEG studies showed
no characteristic features for CJD. All patients were
methionine homozygotes at codon 129 in the PRNP,
with no pathogenic mutations or insertions. None of
these cases was classified as “probable CJD” using
established clinical criteria; neuropathological exami-
nation was essential for diagnosis and classification,
The neuropathological features in all 10 cases
were strikingly similar, although distinct both from
other reported cases of CJD in young patients (10,
16, 53, 64, 67) and typical cases of sporadic CJD in
elderly patients (6, 15, 19). The most striking abnor-
mality was the presence of multiple amyloid plaques
in a widespread distribution involving the cerebral

This possibility has recently
been reinforced by experimental transmission studies
of BSE by intracerebral inoculation into macaque
monkeys (55). Neuropathological studies on these
animal revealed a similar pattern of lesions to those
of vCJD, including amyloid plaques surrounded by
spongiform change in the cerebrum (Figure 9). The
BSE agent appears to have been responsible for the
occurrence of novel forms of TSE in other species as a
consequence of exposure by the oral route (62),
which has been sufficient to overcome the “species
barrier” to transmission (Table 2). Final assessment of
the relationship between BSE and vCJD in terms of
their causative agents awaits the results of strain typ-
ing studies in mice, which have so far revealed a sin-
gle agent strain in various cases of BSE and related
disorders in ungulates, domestic and wild cats (23). What is the Basis for Phenotypic Variation in CJD7
A number of factors exist which might potential-
ly influence the disease phenotype in sporadic CJD;
these can be broadly subdivided into host and agent
factors. From experimental TSE studies, it is known
that host genotype is of major importance in deter-
mining disease phenotype and that the PRNP is the
major influencing factor (26, 35). Recent studies of
human PRNP genotype have found that the naturally
occurring polymorphism at codon 129 is of major
importance in determining disease phenotype (33,
56), in addition to acting as a susceptibility factor for
both sporadic and iatrogenic CJD (29,68). The pres-
ence of one or two valine alleles at codon 129 in
Caucasian populations is strongly correlated with the
presence of PrPres plaques in the brain (33); similar
findings have been reported in the Japanese popula-

The presence of abundant PrPres plaques in vCJD ( all
cases of which so far have occurred in methionine
homozygotes) reinforces the distinction between this
disorder and typical sporadic CJD (83). An increasing number of disease-associated rnuta-
tions have been identified in the human PRNP gene,
many of which are associated with characteristic
clinical and pathological features (3, 18, 25, 41, 49,
60, 73). However, it is worthwhile to note that even
with individual families, there is often a considerable
degree of phenotypic variation within a particular
inherited form of TSE (28, 43); this variability does
not appear to be associated with co-existing codon
129 polymorphisms, and is of uncertain etiology. Attempts have been made to study the potential
effects of other human genes on CJD, particularly the
ApoE gene (1, 66, 70). Although this gene appears to
be a major importance in determining susceptibility
to Alzheimer's disease, studies of CJD have not in
general supported the concept of ApoE as a major
risk factor, particularly in relation to age at disease
onset. In typical cases of sporadic CJD, the age of the
patient has little influence on clinical or pathological
features, although there appears to be a tendency for
the youngest reported patients to have a longer dura-
tion of illness (10, 16, 22, 53, 64, 67). In iatrogenic CJD, it is possible to identify two
general clinical subgroups according to the route of
inoculation of the transmissible agent (21). In cases
with central inoculation (stereotactic electrodes,
corneal transplants, neurosurgical instruments and
dura mater grafts) the clinical and pathological fea-
tures resemble those of typical sporadic CJD with a
short clinical history, a presentation with rapid
dementia, characteristic EEG changes and spongi-
form change present predominantly in the cerebrum
(21,58).

In cases
with central inoculation (stereotactic electrodes,
corneal transplants, neurosurgical instruments and
dura mater grafts) the clinical and pathological fea-
tures resemble those of typical sporadic CJD with a
short clinical history, a presentation with rapid
dementia, characteristic EEG changes and spongi-
form change present predominantly in the cerebrum
(21,58). In contrast, cases with peripheral inocula-
tion of the transmissible agent (hGH and pituitary
gonadotrophin recipients) usually exhibit a pro-
longed clinical history with cerebellar signs and
symptoms on presentation, no characteristic EEG
changes and dementia only present in the final
stages of the disease (11, 21, 78). In these cases, the
most severe pathology is identified in the cerebellum
which shows severe neuronal loss, astrocytosis and
spongiform change, with PrPre5 plaques identified in
the cerebellar cortex and white matter, and in the
cerebrum. Spongiform change, neuronal loss and
astrocytosis are usually prominent in the basal gan-
glia but less conspicuous in the cerebral cortex (9,ll). Recent studies of relative
concentrations in the
cerebrum and cerebellum have reinforced the "target-

and have led to the suggestion that such diffeIences
may also result from the selection of specific strains
of the transmissible agent responsible for this disease
(3 7). In contrast to scrapie, where around 20 different
strains of the transmissible agent have been identi-

Although spongiform change, neuronal loss,
astrocytosis and amyloid plaque formation are the
classical neuropathological features of TSE, none are

Relationship of CJD to Other Dementias
Although spongiform change, neuronal loss,
astrocytosis and amyloid plaque formation are the
classical neuropathological features of TSE, none are
in themselves specific for this group of disorders (9). Vacuolation of the cerebral cortex indistinguishable
from spongiform change has been described in
Alzheimer’s disease and in diffuse Lewy body disease
(although in a restricted distribution usually involv-
ing the temporal lobe) (44), whilst in CJD spongi-
form change is usually evident in the basal ganglia,
thalamus and cerebellum to varying degrees (9, 24). Neuronal loss and astrocytosis are of course common
in many primary and acquired neurodegenerative
disorders and amyloid plaques are a prominent fea-
ture in the pathology of Alzheimer’s disease,
although the amyloid in this disease is derived from
another cell surface glycoprotein, the P-amyloid pre-
cursor protein. Morphological studies of P r P s and
AP amyloid plaques have identified structural simi-
larities (71), particularly with respect to the role of
microglial cells (5, 62); AP protein can be deposited
at the periphery of PrPres plaques in human TSE (25,
63). On the basis of these observations, it has been
suggested that similar disease mechanisms may oper-
ate in Alzheimer’s disease and human TSE, despite
their differing etiology (34, 71). Further interest in
the interrelationship of these disorders is prompted
by the observation that P-amyloid accumulation can
be induced by experimental inoculation of Alzheimer
brain material into the marmoset brain (4). Further
studies are required to establish whether this phe-
nomenon is simply a consequence of amyloid seed-
ing (31, 47), or whether other as yet unidentified fac-
tors are involved. J.W. Ironside: Review: Creutzieldt-Jakob Disease

Earlier reports of a “prion dementia without char-
acteristic pathology” in a young individual in a fami-
ly with a 144 bp mutation in the PRNP gene prompt-
ed speculation on the relationship of human TSE to
other dementias, particularly those with atypical
clinical and histological features (28). Whilst earlier
apocalyptic visions (2) of large numbers of hidden
cases of human TSE have not been supported over
subsequent years (ZO), it is now opportune to reassess
the relationship between the extremes of phenotypic
variability in human TSE and other human demen-
tias which are difficult to classify on standard clinical
and neuropathological criteria. A detailed assess-
ment of this difficult field would provide useful
information to delineate accurately the clinical and
pathological spectrum of human TSE, and might also
provide valuable data on other rare forms of demen-
tia. Such an exercise need not of course be confined
to the elderly population; enigmatic neurodegenera-
tive disorders such as Alpers’ disease (57) would also
benefit from rigorous reassessment using modern
investigative techniques.

benefit from rigorous reassessment using modern
investigative techniques. Conclusion
The current resurgence of interest in CJD and
related disorders provides an opportunity to under-
take work which will help define the clinical and
pathological spectrum of this group of disorders and
allow a better understanding of disease pathogenesis. Whilst this work must be viewed in the light of
ongoing scientific studies into the nature of the
transmissible agents responsible for these disorders,
their means of propagation and disease initiation,
the emergence of an apparently new variant of
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in the UK and subsequently
in France has highlighted the need for further com-
parative studies between human and animal TSE. The recent political and economic consequences of
this recent discovery have highlighted the funda-
mental importance of neuropathology as a diagnos-
tic and research tool in this field. This has given a
unique impetus to our speciality which should not
be missed, as it provides the framework for an oppor-
tunity to undertake medical and scientific studies
which are of potentially major significance for the
UK and elsewhere. Acknowledgements

INTRODUCTION

my /n October 1997, Stanley Prusiner, a professor at the University
of California-San Francisco who had spent twenty-five years studying
prions, went to Stockholm to receive the prize he called “the big one”
from the King of Sweden. His great achievement was to show that the
prion (pronounced “pree-on”), the infectious agent responsible for
bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or mad cow disease, Creutzfeldt-
Jakob disease, and a disease in sheep called scrapie, was not a virus or
a bacterium but a protein, a nonliving thing. Protein, as the name sug-
gests, is prime, proto matter.

source: The Family That Couldnt Sleep a Medical Mystery (D.T. MAX) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
Protein, as the name sug-
gests, is prime, proto matter. (“These agents,” one prion researcher
told a documentary film interviewer, “are almost immortal.”)
The fifty-five-year-old Prusiner’s discovery, the Swedish academy
noted, introduced “a new biological principle of infection” into sci-
ence. Over the years, Prusiner, an ambitious man, had developed a
taste for good wine and food. Now the Swedish elite entertained him at
their finest restaurants while the press pursued him for his photo-
graph and his ideas. The moment was just as he’d always dreamed it
would be. Asked by the newspapers what was left now that he had the
top prize in science, he said his new goal would be to work towards “an
xiv
Introduction
effective therapy for prion diseases.” In 1998, he told an Israeli news-
paper he thought he’d have a cure in five years. Three years later, in 2001, when a family in the Veneto, the Italian
region of small towns and farms outside Venice, held its first family re-
union, Prusiner’s words were on their minds. Family reunions are rare
in Italy, because they are unnecessary: Italian families already do
everything together; you can’t reunite something that never disperses. This family had a special reason for its gatherings, though—many of
its members carry a gene for a dreadful disease. Of noble origin, the
family counts doctors, engineers, industrial managers, and a well-
respected academic among its number. But this family is cursed. For at least two centuries, its members
have suffered from an inherited prion disease called fatal familial in-
somnia that strikes them, usually in their fifties, killing by depriving
them of sleep. FFI is an autosomal dominant mutation, which means
that a child of a parent with FFI has a 50 percent chance of getting
it, too.

source: The Family That Couldnt Sleep a Medical Mystery (D.T. MAX) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
FFI is an autosomal dominant mutation, which means
that a child of a parent with FFI has a 50 percent chance of getting
it, too. In the general population the chance of having FFI is one in
30 million; within the affected branches of this Italian family, it is one
in two. The symptoms of FFI are remarkable and grim. Typically, one day
in middle age, the sufferer finds that he has begun to sweat. A look in
the mirror will show that his pupils have shrunk to pinpricks and he is
holding his head in an odd, stiff way. (I write “he” for clarity, though
men and women are equally affected.) Constipation is common, the
women suddenly enter menopause and the men become impotent. The sufferer begins to have trouble sleeping and tries compensating
with a nap in the afternoon, but to no avail. His blood pressure and
pulse have become elevated and his body is in overdrive. Over the en-

but never succeeding in falling into more than a light stupor. FFI suf-

the agitated dream sleep some people experience just before waking,

but they can’t go deeper to get real rest. Their exhaustion is immense,
beyond comprehension. Once the sufferer can no longer sleep, a downward progression en-

ability to think remains intact; sufferers know what is happening. At
first, they can talk about it and even write down their thoughts. After a
few more months, some lose this level of functioning.

told me, “I used to think Alzheimer’s was the worst disease you could
get. But to see a loved one disintegrate in front of your eyes—and for
that person to know it is happening? Somehow, the fact that it is so
rare makes it even worse, it seems to me. I think now even a car acci-
dent would be less cruel.”
This Italian family is one of a handful of families in the world af-
flicted with fatal familial insomnia. They can trace their disease back
to the mid-eighteenth century, possibly to a Venetian doctor who lived
near the Jewish ghetto, and with certainty from him to an aristocrat in
the Veneto named Giuseppe and down to Vincenzo in the 1880s, Gio-
vanni in the 1910s, Pietro in the 1940s, Assunta, Pierina, and Silvano
in the last three decades of the twentieth century and on to... to
whom? That question hangs over the group at its annual reunions. In a sense, the answer is known.

bring about death before the carriers of the mutation can reproduce,

strikes its sufferers after their childbearing years, and because most
members of this family still decide to have children, FFI will live on
through them. The decision to bring a child into the world who may die
a horrible death in middle age is a difficult one. Bologna weighed this
equation at the time it conducted its genetic tests and decided it would

knowledge no family member has terminated a pregnancy out of fear

when the sufferer begins not to sleep. Sleep is central to us. It’s central to the experience of being human. That every person goes to sleep every night, that we all seek a warm,
safe place to cover and restore ourselves for a third of every day, that
people of every race and every age do this, that we have done it since
before we were Homo sapiens, is amazing. Lying down to sleep is the
Introduction

symbol of ebbing life force, a rehearsal for the day we will lie down and
not get up. Sleep is homeostatic—that is, it is controlled by the body’s internal
balance. When we have slept enough, our body wakes us up, and when
we have not slept enough, it forces us to sleep, a soft unyielding power
pushing us down. When you stay awake too long, you experience a
mussy-headedness, a feeling of going under. Even as you force your
eyes to stay open, sleep is flowing in through your ears and nose and
mouth, rising around your legs and arms, weighing down your head
until your chin drops to your chest.

waking. One of the first things the brain learns is to turn the body off. That sleep is one of the body’s most primal functions makes the fact

perhaps the unconsciousness of sleep is exactly its purpose: sleep ex-

healthier—by improving immune function, repairing damaged tissue,
improving nerve connections. The early-seventeenth-century writer
Richard Burton catalogued its virtues in 7e Anatomy of Melancholy. Sleep, he wrote, “moystens and fattens the body, concocts, and helpes

limbs after long work.” No doubt sleep does this and more, but that

neurosis. Their condition would not seem life-threatening—and yet
Introduction
xix
they too died. What did they die from? No experiment has ever an-
swered that question. Allan Rechtschaffen came close by keeping rats
awake until they died, at around fourteen days. During this time, the
rats overproduced adrenalinelike hormones, in effect going into over-
drive, and underproduced thyroid hormones, used by the body for
weight and temperature control. They ate aggressively but kept losing
weight and their skin began to break down. Eventually, they began to
shiver and they died. Clearly, something had gone wrong with their in-
ternal regulatory functioning—their autonomic nervous system—but
on autopsy, nothing sufficient to explain their deaths was found. It is
almost as if a tautology had killed them: ifyou force a rat to stay awake,
it dies from lack of sleep. Rechtschaffen’s experiment is not a pleasant one to contemplate. To
watch any animal endure insomnia is uncomfortable; to watch a human
suffer from it is horrifying. Many in the Italian family have had this ex-
perience.

Gathered
were about fifty family members, at once embarrassed, nervous, hope-

the meeting, they were admitting that the family had a problem, and
that a concerted effort might find a solution. It was a sunny day, and the flowers were in bloom along the roads
and canals of the Veneto. Sheep and cows grazed in the nearby fields
and locals bicycled back and forth from the markets, ducking around
the traffic barriers at the train crossing. Family members had come
from as far away as Padua, which though only an hour by car, repre-
sented a considerable journey: Italians like to remain in paese, close to
home. Now they gathered in the house of a family member who has lost an
uncle, two aunts, and a grandfather to the disease. The man owns a
small business. He makes good money and he built a new ranch-style
house whose spacious central hall would not be out of place in north-
ern California or the Hamptons. The light pours into his house. He
does not worry or think much about the disease, unlike his sister Eli-
sabetta. This is common among families with genetic diseases: mem-
bers tend to divide between the ignorers and the burden carriers. In
this family, Lisi, as the family calls Elisabetta, is a burden carrier. Be-
fore the meeting she took me on a bike ride down the cypress-lined
lane to the town cemetery, where many of her relatives are buried. We
looked at the pictures of her uncle and her grandfather and she seemed
on the verge of tears. Lisi and her husband, Ignazio, a doctor of internal medicine, were
crucial in the discovery of the disease.

important this meeting could prove for the future of the family and
added that at that moment, fortunately, no one was dying of the dis-

the room was thinking about death, they were also taking comfort in

someone is being unnecessarily brusque or aggressive, they say he is
being “anglosassone,” Anglo-Saxon. The idea of this first reunion was
very anglosassone, spurred by the success that AIDS activists had had

text:
Prion diseases are a fascinating medical mystery, because they ap-
pear to be the only disease that takes those three forms: genetic, infec-
tious, and accidental (often called “sporadic”). The theory of prion
diseases—I write “theory” because the gold standard of proof has not
yet been met—is that prions can perform this triple trick because they
are agents unique in biology: infectious proteins. That is, they are pro-
teins that behave like viruses or bacteria. Until the discovery of prions, scientists thought proteins could not
have this ability. They knew them as the building blocks of the body—
“nature’s robots,” in the dismissive words of one book on them—
things the body made and, when their function was fulfilled, disposed
of. The human body has roughly a hundred thousand different pro-
teins. Hair and muscle are mostly protein; skin is made up of proteins
too. There are also tens of thousands more proteins within the cell
xxvi = /ntroduction
about which we know little or nothing, the functioning of the various
proteins in the body being the last great frontier of human biology. A
recent proteomics conference title caught this sense of challenge:
“Human Proteome Project: “Genes Were Easy.’ ”
Certainly easier than prions. We don’t even know what prions do
when healthy—they may possibly aid in memory; in yeast, they have
been shown to make genetic adaptation easier. Because they can be
found in all mammals, it is safe to assume that they have a function—
otherwise the gene responsible for them would have dropped out or
become inoperative somewhere along the course of animal evolution. How do prions infect their victims? The body manufactures pro-
teins as ribbons, which then fold into three-dimensional shapes that
allow them to fulfill whatever function they have.

source: The Family That Couldnt Sleep a Medical Mystery (D.T. MAX) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
How do prions infect their victims? The body manufactures pro-
teins as ribbons, which then fold into three-dimensional shapes that
allow them to fulfill whatever function they have. Most proteins, be-
cause of the arrangement of their atoms, have only one such shape, but
prion proteins—the theory goes—have two, one normal, the second
infectious and lethal. Once the first abnormal prion appears, it begins to spread in the
body through a process called “conformational influence” —“confor-
mation” meaning “shape.” After one prion becomes malignant, the
way it’s folded allows it to bond with adjoining healthy prion proteins,
and the bonding causes these prion proteins in turn to fold wrongly
and bond with others, making them fold wrongly, too. The chain reac-
tion extends from protein to protein, normal prion protein changing to
lethal prion in a series of Jekyll-to-Hyde conversions. Cells that have
the misformed prions in them sicken and die, for reasons we don’t
really understand, but the effect of all these misfolded proteins on the
delicate cells of the sufferer’s brain is overwhelming: the brain tissue
of prion disease victims is full of gaps, areas where all the cells have
died, as if an explosion had gone off. Writing of her father, who had
died of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, one woman posted on an e-mail list:
“My husband seen his brain X-ray and said it looked like someone shot
him with a .22 shotgun.”
Introduction
xxvii
For biologists the prion theory is a heresy. To them, the word “infec-
tion” means something specific—a disease process brought about by
living things, more exactly by things with nucleic acids or genetic ma-
terial in them. Whatever else proteins are, they are not living and have
no nucleic acid. The theory of prions thus threatens to unmake the
defining moment in biology.

source: The Family That Couldnt Sleep a Medical Mystery (D.T. MAX) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk).pdf
text:
Whatever else proteins are, they are not living and have
no nucleic acid. The theory of prions thus threatens to unmake the
defining moment in biology. In 1862, Louis Pasteur boiled broth to kill
the microscopic life in it, put some of the liquid in a goose-necked
flask, and showed that if nothing living ever reached the liquid, no life
would ever grow there. The experiment had enormous practical im-
pact; it gave doctors the knowledge they still use to save lives by show-
ing that because infections were living, reproducing things, if you
could keep an environment sterile, you could keep a patient healthy. Had infectious prions been in Pasteur’s flask, curative medicine would
never have gotten started. Doctors would still be competing with
shamans and medicasters. Because the possibility that infectious agents don’t have to be alive
violates a paradigm, various prion diseases have been around for a
long time without anyone successfully connecting them. All that doc-
tors and scientists knew before the current effort to find the underly-
ing unifying principle began was what they could see: that there
existed a small group of diseases with roughly similar symptoms, in-
cluding loss of coordination and dementia, and with a perplexing ab-
sence of fever—one expects to see fever in an infection but in prion
diseases one doesn’t. Scientists also saw how these diseases had a ten-
dency to burst into sudden outbreaks and then disappear, but they did
not know why. The fact that the diseases had this ability, though, al-
ways lent urgency to the attempt to understand what was going on.

creased enormously when researchers discovered in the mid-1990s
that a prion disease in cattle—specifically, bovine spongiform en-

cephalopathy, or mad cow disease—could jump the species barrier
and infect humans. The more scientists understood about prion dis-

any living being, start a rapid process of misfolding and infection that
would kill that individual and make its invisible way from one body to
another and from one species to another. The fear of the potency of
prions can be seen in the caution coroners and undertakers use in han-
dling the bodies of prion disease victims. They bury them in nine-foot-
deep graves. They warn the bereaved not to touch their dead. Sometimes they don’t even allow their relatives in the same room as
the closed casket. “The coroner here would not even let us have my
husband’s body,” one woman wrote on a website for the relatives of
prion disease sufferers. “We just had to have a memorial service.”
Itis enormously difficult to disinfect a prion. What kills viruses and
bacteria barely affects them. Boiling will not disinfect them, nor will
heat. You can’t reliably “kill” a prion with radiation. You can’t pour
formaldehyde on it to render it harmless—in fact formaldehyde makes
prions tougher. Not all bleaches can kill prions and those that can need
to be highly concentrated. Prions bond to metal.

Despite the trauma and fear chronicled in these pages, this book is
meant to be, if not a tribute, at least an admiring acknowledgment of
human achievement. Prions and the diseases they cause could not
have been discovered by the research methods that so often dominate
modern science. It required remarkable men and women making great
imaginative leaps to build the theory of prion diseases. Two of these
scientists—Carleton Gajdusek, who studied a tribe in Papua New
Guinea afflicted with a prion disease called kuru that nearly extermi-
nated them—and Stanley Prusiner at UC-San Francisco, who helped
identify the key protein and then named it—won Nobel Prizes for their
efforts. This book cannot do other than to admire their work and what
it suggests about human potential, the interrogative, investigative,
imaginative impulse that has made Homo sapiens the dominant ani-
mal on the planet.

and chronic wasting disease in our own times (and even a prion epi-
